title: dramatic monologue|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The Iron Lung  

The doors hiss shut—a gasp, a choke—  
and we are sealed in steel and sweat.  
No breath escapes; the air is thick  
with yesterday’s coffee, damp wool,  
the sour tang of exhaustion,  
and something older: fear, or faith,  
or just the slow surrender  
of bodies pressed too close to care.  

A man leans, slack-jawed, against the pole—  
his eyes open, unseeing,  
as if his soul has already alighted  
three stops ago.  
A woman grips her bag like a shield,  
knuckles white, gaze fixed on the ad  
for vacations she’ll never take.  
A child whimpers, muffled by a coat,  
while his mother stares straight ahead—  
not at the map, not at the ads,  
but *through* them, into some hollow  
where silence has weight and volume.  

We sway as one organism—  
a lung inhaling, exhaling,  
never filling.  
The train groans, brakes shriek,  
and for one suspended second,  
we all hold our breath—not in awe,  
but in the ancient, animal hush  
before the fall.  

And when the voice crackles,  
*“Next stop: Grand Central,”*  
no one moves.  
We don’t believe it.  
We’ve heard that name before—  
a promise whispered in every tunnel,  
a station we pass through  
but never truly reach.  

We are commuters.  
Not travelers. Not pilgrims.  
Just breath held,  
just bone and busyness,  
riding the iron lung  
that pulses us, pulse by pulse,  
deeper into the dark—  
toward work, toward home,  
toward something we call *later*,  
though later keeps receding  
like the tunnel wall behind us:  
always there,  
always gone.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|hope after a long illness
text:
In the ward where machines hum like a chorus line,
And the scent of disinfectant is perfume,
I found hope in the most unlikely sign—
A spider, weaving through the sterile gloom.

Its web, a fragile lace across the light,
Caught sunbeams, spun them into golden thread.
Each strand a whisper, each knot a promise bright,
A map of resilience, finely etched and spread.

For weeks, I watched it build, this tiny architect,
Crafting a home from thin air and resolve.
While I, entangled in my own quiet sect,
Learned to breathe again, to dream, to evolve.

Now, as I step out, the world seems new,
With every breath, a filament of blue.

title: ode|moving out of a childhood home
text:
Ode to the Departing Key  

Not with a slam, but silence—soft and deep—  
I turn the brass one last time in the lock,  
That cold, familiar weight I used to keep  
Safe in my palm, a talisman, a shock  
Of childhood’s claim. The hallway breathes its dust,  
Sunlight suspended in the slanting air,  
Each grain of wood, each crack in plaster’s thrust,  
Holds decades like a slow, unbroken prayer.  

The kitchen floor still bears the ghostly stain  
Of spilled grape juice and Sunday pancake flour;  
The stairs remember every leap, each strain  
Of teenage sighs that climbed toward the tower  
Of bedroom dreams. The windowpane reflects  
Not just my face—but smaller, barefoot, wide-eyed,  
A boy who thought this roof would always protect  
The world he knew, where all his truths abided.  

Now boxes wait like coffins, neatly sealed,  
Their tape a shroud for toys, for letters, books,  
For trophies rusting, promises concealed  
In drawers half-empty, trembling at the looks  
Of strangers soon to walk these creaking floors.  
I trace the doorframe—where my height was scored—  
A jagged line no ruler could restore,  
A map of growth I never paused to record.  

Oh, house—not brick, nor beam, nor pane, nor door,  
But vessel: holding love too vast to name—  
You taught me shelter, then you taught me more:  
How love expands when it releases flame.  
So I release you. Not with grief, but grace—  
This key, now lighter, fits no lock but space.

title: ghazal|the first heartbreak
text:
My coffee’s gone cold again—third cup, same stain  
on the chipped mug you gave me, blue as your raincoat that day.  

I still check my phone at 3:17 a.m., though your number’s blocked  
and your sister’s cat—Mittens—still sleeps on my couch, tail twitching.  

You left your green scarf draped over the banister.  
I haven’t moved it. Not even when the landlord came to fix the leak.  

Remember how we’d split the last slice of cherry pie at Pete’s Diner?  
The crust always broke unevenly—like us, you said, and laughed.  

Your laugh lives in the hallway now. Or maybe it’s just the pipes groaning.  
The radiator hisses like steam escaping a cracked valve.  

I wore your father’s old flannel shirt to the funeral last week—  
not yours. His. Mine. It smells like mothballs and something faintly sweet.  

Some nights I hum the wrong verse of “Hallelujah,”  
stop mid-line, and stare at the ceiling fan’s slow, lopsided spin.

title: prose poem|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Beneath the silvered gaze of the moon,  
A camp stirs, whispers in the night,  
Tents like shadows, a sea of quiet dreams,  
Under the vast, indifferent sky.

The moon, a silent sentinel, casts its light,  
Over faces marked by miles and years,  
Eyes that have seen too much, yet still hold hope,  
In the soft, forgiving glow of lunar beams.

Children sleep, their breaths a gentle lullaby,  
To the restless earth beneath their makeshift beds,  
Dreaming, perhaps, of homes left behind,  
Of laughter echoing through familiar streets.

Mothers keep watch, their hearts a steady drum,  
Beating against the cold, relentless fear,  
Fathers, with hands that once built and sowed,  
Now cradle memories, as precious as gold.

And there, amidst the silence, life persists,  
Like the wildflowers pushing through cracked earth,  
Finding beauty in the most unlikely places,  
Hope, in the face of an unyielding world.

The moon, a witness to this fragile dance,  
Between despair and the indomitable will,  
Gives no answers, only its gentle light,  
A companion in the long, lonely night.

title: poem in tercets|the ocean during a storm
text:
I. The Gathering  
The sky bruises purple at the rim,  
a held breath before the gale’s first cry—  
waves coil like serpents, thick and dim.  

Wind snatches foam from crests too high,  
the gulls retreat to cliff-led ledges,  
and salt stings the tongue like a lie.  

II. The Breaking  
The horizon shatters—black and wedges  
of water heave, then crash and rend;  
lightning stitches the dark with edges.  

The hull groans, bent and nearly bent,  
as troughs become abyssal graves—  
each wave a god who will not relent.  

III. The After  
Dawn bleeds thin on water’s raves,  
foam dissolves like spent regret;  
the sea exhales in silver waves.  

Gulls return, their cries unmet  
by thunder—only gulls, and light,  
and what the deep has kept, and kept.

title: elegy|a mother's hands
text:
Elegy for the Hands

Not the knuckles, swollen as river stones,  
but the way they held a spool of thread—  
not sewing, just holding it,  
the blue plastic reel balanced on the pad  
of her thumb, turning slow,  
a tiny planet she refused to let spin.  

The way they folded laundry:  
not smoothing, but *tucking*—  
her fingers sliding deep into the damp sleeve  
of my old flannel shirt,  
pushing the cuff inward like a secret  
she’d already forgotten.  

The way they gripped the steering wheel  
at 3 a.m., headlights cutting fog,  
not white-knuckled, but loose—  
left hand resting at nine, right at three,  
as if conducting silence,  
her palms slightly damp, smelling of cold metal  
and the faint, metallic tang of the Band-Aid  
she’d peeled off that morning,  
leaving a ghost-circle of adhesive  
on the webbing between thumb and forefinger.  

The way they stirred soup—not clockwise, not steady—  
but in short, impatient jabs,  
like a mechanic testing a spark plug’s resistance,  
the wooden spoon tapping the pot’s rim:  
*tick-tick-tick*,  
a Morse code for *I’m still here*,  
though the broth went cold twice.  

The way they rested, finally,  
on the hospital sheet—  
not crossed, not folded,  
but splayed, open,  
fingertips pointing east,  
as if waiting for a signal  
from a satellite no one else could see,  
their veins like faded ink  
on tracing paper,  
their nails—chipped, unvarnished—  
still holding the shadow  
of yesterday’s garden soil  
beneath the second-to-last nail  
on the left hand.  

I press my palm to the hollow where hers lay.  
The sheet is warm.  
The warmth is not hers.  
It is only the room remembering heat.

title: villanelle|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
A Lost Glove on a Fence Post

A lonely glove, upon the fence, does rest,  
Where winds and whispers of the fields converge.  
Its pair, in some forgotten place, is lost.

What hands it warmed, what tales it might attest,  
Of labor done, or loves that did emerge?  
A lonely glove, upon the fence, does rest.

The sun sets low, casting shadows long,  
In twilight's hush, secrets softly tossed.  
Its pair, in some forgotten place, is lost.

Now frost bites deep with winter's icy test,  
Yet still it clings where once it could disperse.  
A lonely glove, upon the fence, does rest.

Perhaps in dreams, its mate it will invest,  
Through nights that hold the promise to be crossed.  
Its pair, in some forgotten place, is lost.

So here it stays, in quiet dignity,  
A sentinel of seasons, undeterred.  
A lonely glove, upon the fence, does rest.  
Its pair, in some forgotten place, is lost.

title: pantoum|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The landline rang—three sharp, old-fashioned tones,  
like Dad’s knuckles rapping the kitchen door.  
I almost didn’t answer—thought it was debts or loans,  
or Mrs. Gable asking about her dog once more.  

Like Dad’s knuckles rapping the kitchen door,  
I fumbled the cordless, sticky with jam from breakfast toast.  
Mrs. Gable asking about her dog once more—  
then your voice: “Hey. It’s me. I’m not dead. Just… mostly lost.”  

I fumbled the cordless, sticky with jam from breakfast toast,  
and dropped the receiver—clatter, then static hiss.  
“Just… mostly lost.” You said it like a ghost  
who’d forgotten how to hold a phone, or wish.  

The static hiss hung there, thin as that blue sweater  
you wore the summer you slept in the garage,  
the one with the moth hole near the left cuff—  
I still have it folded, somewhere, in a box marked *Garage*.  

You wore the blue sweater the summer you slept in the garage,  
said Mom’s new boyfriend smelled like burnt toast and shame.  
I still have it folded, somewhere, in a box marked *Garage*,  
and your old baseball glove, stiff with dried rain.  

Burnt toast and shame—that’s what the line kept breathing,  
while I stared at the fridge, its magnet holding up  
a grocery list in your handwriting: *milk, batteries,  
a real apology, if you’re still breathing*.  

A real apology, if you’re still breathing—  
you laughed, a short, dry sound, like gravel shifting.  
I stared at the fridge, its magnet holding up  
a photo of us, eight and ten, grinning, missing teeth.  

Gravel shifting. Then silence. Not empty—thick, like steam  
off the kettle last night, when I boiled water for tea  
and forgot to pour it, just watched the lid tremble,  
steam rising, rising, no one there to see.

title: elegy|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
Elegy for the Last Watch  

The lamp still turns—  
a slow, bronze eye unblinking—  
casting its long arm across the black water,  
sweeping the same arc it has swept for forty years:  
*shoreward, seaward, shoreward*,  
like a prayer worn smooth by repetition.  

He sits at the base of the tower,  
boots unlaced, cap in his lap,  
the brass buttons cold as drowned coins.  
Outside, the gale combs the cliffs with salt and fury,  
but inside—only the *tick-tick-tick*  
of the clockwork heart,  
and the low hum of glass warming,  
of oil burning clean and quiet,  
as if the light itself were holding its breath.  

He traces the grooves in the oak banister—  
notches carved for each storm survived,  
each ship guided home, each child born far inland,  
each letter folded thin with distance.  
His hands remember rope, rust, brine,  
the weight of the lens when he cleaned it at dawn,  
the way the beam would catch a gull’s wing mid-flight—  
a sudden silver stitch in the grey.  

At 3:17 a.m.,  
he climbs—not to tend, but to witness.  
Steps worn concave by decades of ascent.  
Up past the gallery where fog once stole his voice,  
up past the storm-lantern’s ghostly halo,  
up into the lantern room,  
where the great Fresnel lens hangs like a frozen galaxy,  
prisms catching the last of his shadow—  
long, lean, trembling just once  
as he lays his palm flat against the warm glass.  

No farewell. No flourish.  
Just the light, still turning.  
Still reaching.  
Still *there*.  

When the relief arrives at first light,  
they find the stool drawn close to the railing,  
his coat draped over it, collar turned up against the wind—  
as if he’d stepped out for air,  
and the sea, in its ancient courtesy,  
had simply taken him mid-breath,  
leaving only the lamp,  
still turning,  
still turning,  
still turning—  
a solitary grammar of grace  
in the grammarless dark.

title: pantoum|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
Whispers of Cinnamon

In her kitchen, cinnamon dances on air,  
Stories simmer in pots, warm and fair.  
Cookies crumble, a sweet, golden hue,  
Where love lingers, in everything she brew.

Echoes of Soup

Stories simmer in pots, warm and fair,  
Her hands move like poetry, with care.  
Where love lingers, in everything she brew,  
Aromas weave through the old and the new.

Silent Recipes

Her hands move like poetry, with care,  
Cookies crumble, a sweet, golden hue.  
Aromas weave through the old and the new,  
In her kitchen, cinnamon dances on air.

title: free verse poem|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
Behind the Swing Door

Steam rises like a ghost from the stainless steel sink,  
a slow exhale of yesterday’s onions, today’s basil,  
the sharp tang of lemon zest clinging to our aprons.  

We count forks—not vows—  
thirty-seven salad tongs laid out in perfect alignment,  
each one wiped twice: once for shine, once for silence.  

The muffled swell of strings leaks through the wall—  
not music, but pressure: a tremor in the floorboards,  
a vibration in the wine glasses stacked three high on the pass.  

She stumbles in, veil askew, laughing breathlessly,  
asks for ice, then changes her mind, asks for water,  
then vanishes again—leaving only the scent of gardenias  
and the faintest smudge of lipstick on the edge of a champagne flute  
we’ll wash before she even knows it’s gone.  

He follows later, tie loosened, eyes wide and unmoored,  
leans against the fridge, whispers *“Do you think they’ll notice if the cake leans?”*  
We nod. We don’t look up. We pipe buttercream roses  
with steady hands, each petal a small act of faith  
in gravity, in sugar, in the illusion of control.  

The toast blares through the intercom—  
a crackle, then laughter, then applause like rain on tin.  
We lift our spoons in salute, not to love, but to timing:  
the precise second the risotto hits the plate,  
the exact degree the duck breast yields beneath the knife.  

Later, when the last guest sways into the night,  
we sweep crumbs from the floor—petals, rice, a single pearl earring,  
a dropped cufflink shaped like a crescent moon.  
No one sees us fold the napkins back into origami doves,  
or how we taste the leftover frosting—sweet, salted, real—  
before turning off the lights,  
leaving the kitchen empty,  
except for the hum of the walk-in,  
and the quiet, stubborn warmth  
of something that was made,  
served,  
and loved—  
if only by the hands that held it first.

title: pantoum|an abandoned railway station
text:
Abandoned Station  

The platform wears a coat of rust and rain,  
Weeds pierce the cracks where ticket booths once stood.  
A single bench leans, bent with silent strain,  
Its green paint peeled like old, unkept vows.  

Weeds pierce the cracks where ticket booths once stood,  
A clock hangs frozen at ten minutes past three.  
Its green paint peeled like old, unkept vows,  
While sparrows nest in hollowed timbers, free.  

A clock hangs frozen at ten minutes past three,  
Wind hums through shattered glass and splintered beams.  
While sparrows nest in hollowed timbers, free,  
And echo lingers—ghosts of vanished dreams.  

Wind hums through shattered glass and splintered beams,  
A rusted sign still whispers “Next Stop: Home.”  
And echo lingers—ghosts of vanished dreams,  
But no train comes; the tracks are overgrown.  

A rusted sign still whispers “Next Stop: Home.”  
The platform wears a coat of rust and rain.  
But no train comes; the tracks are overgrown.  
A single bench leans, bent with silent strain.

title: villanelle|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
Above the frozen lake, a V cuts through,
The geese in flight, a map of old desires.
My breath turns to frost as I watch them pursue.

Their calls echo, a haunting, distant tune,
A song that speaks of places far and near.
Above the frozen lake, a V cuts through,

And in their wake, the silence seems to swoon,
The ice beneath, a canvas stark and clear.
My breath turns to frost as I watch them pursue.

I think of you, your laughter, your perfume,
How we once danced beneath the winter sky.
Above the frozen lake, a V cuts through,

But now the stars are cold, the moon a loom,
Weaving shadows where our dreams did lie.
My breath turns to frost as I watch them pursue.

The geese will find their haven, safe and true,
While I stand here, under this vast, dark sigh.
Above the frozen lake, a V cuts through,
My breath turns to frost as I watch them pursue.

title: elegy|a soldier writing home
text:
Letter from the Trenches, October 1917  

The ink bleeds where my thumb smudges the page—  
a slow bruise on cheap, yellowed paper.  
Outside, rain stitches the mud with silver thread,  
and the poppies won’t bloom here—not yet.  

I fold the letter twice, then once more,  
as if pressing grief into a book of pressed violets.  
My pen rests where your name begins: *Eleanor*,  
three syllables I trace like rosary beads—  
soft, sacred, trembling in the candle’s thin light.  

The rifle leans against the sandbag, cold and faithful.  
Its barrel holds the sky’s last grey—  
not the blue you painted on our bedroom wall,  
but the colour of unopened letters,  
of teacups left too long on the sill.  

I write that the larks still sing at dawn—  
true, though their notes are thin as wire,  
snagged on barbed wire, on wind, on silence.  
I do not write how Private Hemlock coughed all night,  
or how the earth smells like wet iron and turned root.  

I sign *Yours, always*,  
then pause—my hand hovering, ink pooling  
like a small, dark pond above your name.  
Somewhere, a train whistles—low, far off—  
the same one that carried me past the station oak,  
past the swing set swaying empty in the wind.  

The candle gutters.  
I seal the envelope with wax the colour of dried blood,  
and press my thumbprint deep—  
not as signature, but as soil,  
as seed,  
as something I leave behind  
that might, one day,  
push green through the frost.

title: elegy|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I. Salt and Silence  
The dunes exhale at dusk—cold, slow, and deep—  
as if the earth itself were holding breath.  
No leaf, no bird, no murmur in the sweep  
of wind-scoured stone. Just sand, and time, and death  
unfurling like a scroll no hand can trace.  
Then—first star: a pinprick, sharp and thin,  
piercing the violet hush. A fragile grace,  
a needle-thread of light pulled through the skin  
of night. I name it, though it does not hear.  
It blinks—not in reply, but in its course—  
a distant, dying fire, yet burning clear  
above this hollow, unrelenting source  
of thirst and stillness. I stand small and bare,  
and learn how bright the dark can be—and spare.  

II. The Cartographer’s Lament  
I map them nightly—not with ink or line,  
but with the ache behind my hollow eyes:  
Orion’s belt, the Scorpion’s cruel sign,  
the Dipper’s ladle spilling ancient skies.  
But names dissolve like salt on tongue, like dew  
on sun-baked clay. What good is chart or claim  
when constellations shift, and stars renew  
their burn while we are dust, and ash, and flame?  
A nomad once traced Vega on his palm,  
his thumb a compass, wrist a trembling shore—  
now only wind rewrites the desert’s calm,  
erasing every mark, and asking more:  
What use is memory when light arrives  
from graves older than language, older than lives?  

III. Ashes to Starlight  
At dawn, the sky bleeds pale—a bruise, a sigh—  
the stars grow faint, then fade, then cease to be.  
The dunes exhale again, and so do I,  
a breath as brief as any galaxy.  
Yet last night’s light still travels—far, unseen—  
through vacuum, void, and centuries untold.  
It does not vanish; only shifts, serene,  
from sight to story, silver into gold  
woven in bone, in dust, in whispered prayer.  
So let me rest where heat and silence meet:  
no tomb, no stone—just air, and space, and air—  
my atoms rising, restless, bittersweet,  
to join the drift, the fall, the slow return—  
not gone, but scattered, luminous, and stern.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
Upon a Lake of Ice, the Geese Take Flight

Upon a lake where winter's breath doth lay,
And crystal sheets in moonlit silence gleam,
A flock of geese, in V-form'd array,
Doth pierce the sky, a fleeting, feathered dream.

Their wings, like oars that stir the frozen air,
With every stroke, a whisper to the night,
They seek the south, where warmer climes declare
A refuge from the cold's unyielding bite.

Yet in their passing, grace and beauty blend,
As if the heavens sent these creatures down,
To paint upon the icy canvas, send
A message 'cross the barren, frosty town.

Thus nature weaves her tapestry so fine,
In flight of geese, 'tis poetry divine.

title: dramatic monologue|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The fridge doesn’t hum—it *holds its breath*.  
A low, wet vibration in the floorboards, like a whale’s ribcage  
pressed against basement concrete.  

I stand barefoot on the linoleum’s cold tongue,  
watching the light inside bloom—sudden, surgical—  
as if the thing had been waiting for my hand  
to trigger its small, white godhead.  

The milk carton sweats condensation like a nervous witness.  
Carrots glow orange under plastic, absurdly lit,  
like evidence left at a crime scene no one reported.  
That half-eaten apple? Its flesh has gone matte,  
a tiny, bruised moon refusing to reflect anything.  

I don’t want food. I want the *before* of sound—  
that split-second hush when the compressor cuts,  
when the house exhales and the walls remember they’re wood,  
not just hollows full of wiring and dread.  

But then—the *thrum* returns. Not from the motor.  
From the *space between* the coils: a subsonic tremor  
in the air itself, thick as wet wool,  
making the spoon in the drawer *twitch*  
just once—metal remembering magnetism,  
or maybe just fatigue.  

Outside, the streetlamp blinks—not flicker, but *stutter*,  
like a synapse misfiring in slow motion.  
I count the seconds between pulses: 3.7, 3.9, 4.1…  
My pulse answers back, not in my wrist,  
but behind my left ear—  
a tiny, frantic moth beating against the skull’s thin wall.  

The fridge doesn’t keep time.  
It *steals* it—  
siphons the minutes through its rubber gasket,  
leaves them coiled, cold and silver,  
in the drain pan beneath.  

I close the door.  
Darkness floods back—not black, but *bruised*:  
indigo with a tinge of burnt umber,  
the exact color of the vein on the underside of my wrist  
when I tilt it just so.  

And the hum doesn’t stop.  
It migrates—in through the soles of my feet,  
up the shins, into the hollows behind the knees,  
until my bones are tuning forks  
vibrating at the frequency of absence.  

I am not awake.  
I am *unmoored*—  
a life raft adrift in the warm, slow current  
of the refrigerator’s held breath.

title: blank verse meditation|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
Three a.m. again. The ceiling fan’s slow wobble—  
not quite silent, not quite sound—just air  
stirring the dust motes above the dresser  
where my grandmother’s cracked porcelain clock  
still ticks, though the hands froze at 4:17  
last Tuesday. I count breaths, then stop counting  
when I realize I’m counting the gaps  
between them.  

The fridge kicks on downstairs.  
That low, tired hum—not a drone, exactly,  
but a shudder in the floorboards, a vibration  
in the fillings of my back teeth.  
I know its cadence: the slight rise before  
the compressor groans, the way it drops  
a half-tone when the freezer defrosts—  
like someone clearing their throat in the dark.  

Last night I opened it just to hear it louder.  
Light flared—blinding, absurd—illuminating  
the half-eaten container of takeout lo mein,  
the expired yogurt with the lid slightly puffed,  
and the single, sad tangerine I bought  
thinking I’d eat it *today*, but didn’t.  
Its skin was already dimpling at the stem.  

I closed the door. The hum settled back in,  
deeper now, like it knew something  
I wasn’t saying out loud.  
Like it remembered the weight of my elbow  
on the counter at eleven,  
the exact shade of yellow in the kitchen light  
when I boiled water for tea I never drank.  

Outside, a neighbor’s cat yowls—  
not urgent, just bored.  
The clock still hasn’t moved.  
My left foot’s asleep.  
The hum doesn’t care.  
It just holds the house together,  
low and constant,  
while I lie here,  
listening to the silence between its pulses.

title: villanelle|the first heartbreak
text:
In the garden where our laughter used to bloom,  
Beneath the willow's whisper and the moon's glow,  
Your silence now a chisel, carving gloom.

The echoes of your footsteps fade too soon,  
A symphony of shadows in the room,  
In the garden where our laughter used to bloom.

Leaves rustle like secrets, once shared, now doom,  
Each petal falls, a tear from love’s cocoon,  
Your silence now a chisel, carving gloom.

I trace the path where hand in hand we swoon,  
But only cold air answers my heart's tune,  
In the garden where our laughter used to bloom.

The night wraps tighter, suffocating, consuming,  
Stars mock with their twinkle, as I resume,  
Your silence now a chisel, carving gloom.

Alone, I stand, amidst memories, assuming,  
That time may heal, yet leaves me to consume,  
In the garden where our laughter used to bloom,  
Your silence now a chisel, carving gloom.

title: villanelle|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
I. Smokestacks Stand Silent  
The smokestacks stand silent, tall and thin,  
No greasy steam now curls to meet the gray.  
The whistle’s gone—the shift has ended in.  

The loading docks are choked with rust and gin,  
Where freight cars waited for the break of day.  
The smokestacks stand silent, tall and thin.  

The foreman’s office holds a dusty pin—  
A badge that reads *“Pride”* in faded spray.  
The whistle’s gone—the shift has ended in.  

Boots no longer track the grease-stained din;  
Just pigeons nest where rivets used to stay.  
The smokestacks stand silent, tall and thin.  

The river runs, but not the pay it’s been—  
No overtime, no bonus, no delay.  
The whistle’s gone—the shift has ended in.  

We watch the clouds move slow above the skin  
Of concrete cracked where children used to play.  
The smokestacks stand silent, tall and thin.  
The whistle’s gone—the shift has ended in.  

II. Main Street Hollow  
Main Street hollow, windows taped and thin,  
The diner’s sign flickers one last word: *“Open.”*  
Its booths hold ghosts who never clocked back in.  

The barber’s chair sits tilted, dust within,  
A calendar stuck on October—damp and sullen.  
Main Street hollow, windows taped and thin.  

The hardware store sold nails, then gave up sin—  
Now sells only wind through broken door-frames, muffled.  
Its booths hold ghosts who never clocked back in.  

A teen kicks cans past where the union pin  
Was pinned beside the bank’s old vault, unshut.  
Main Street hollow, windows taped and thin.  

Her mother folds a layoff letter, thin  
As tissue, keeps it pressed inside her apron.  
Its booths hold ghosts who never clocked back in.  

At dusk, the streetlights blink—but not for kin,  
Just static hum where hope once rose and leapt.  
Main Street hollow, windows taped and thin.  
Its booths hold ghosts who never clocked back in.  

III. River Takes the Name  
The river takes the name we used to keep—  
*“Clearwater,”* though copper still runs deep.  
It carries what the furnaces let slip.  

We named our sons for steel, our daughters, “Sheep”  
(For wool from mills that no one tends or keeps).  
The river takes the name we used to keep.  

Old Mr. Varga walks the bank to weep,  
His boots half-sunk where slag and silt congeal.  
It carries what the furnaces let slip.  

The schoolhouse mural fades—a gear, asleep;  
beneath it, chalked in haste: *“We still believe.”*  
The river takes the name we used to keep.  

No sirens rise, no hoot, no clang, no sweep  
Of cranes at dawn—just current, low and steep.  
It carries what the furnaces let slip.  

We whisper names the river won’t release:  
*“Rustbelt,” “Ghostown,” “What We Used to Keep.”*  
The river takes the name we used to keep.  
It carries what the furnaces let slip.

title: ghazal|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean’s Wrath  

The ocean roars—a throat of shattered glass,  
Each wave a fist that strikes the sky’s gray mass.  

Lightning stitches cracks across the deep,  
While thunder hums its ancient, ragged bass.  

Salt stings like grief upon the wind’s raw tongue,  
And every crest is crowned with ghostly lace.  

The hull groans low, a prayer half-drowned in foam,  
As stars retreat behind the tempest’s face.  

No lighthouse holds the dark; no chart can trace  
The path where drowned men kiss the drowning space.  

O tide, you rise not to embrace—but claim:  
All shores are borrowed, all our anchors grace.

title: prose poem|grief after a dog dies
text:
In the quiet after, the house whispers your absence like a hollow shell. I find your echoes in the creaks of the old floorboards, each one a ghostly pawprint trailing through the silence. The sun, a lazy gold coin, slips through the blinds, casting stripes on the carpet where you used to stretch, belly up, paws twitching in some dream of endless fields.

Your collar hangs from the doorknob, a silent bell, its jingle stilled. I touch it, and it feels like a promise unfulfilled, a circle broken. In the kitchen, the water bowl sits empty, a small, dry ocean, its surface a mirror that no longer reflects your eager face. I fill it anyway, a ritual, a futile offering to the void.

Outside, the world is a tapestry of smells without you, a feast of scents you can no longer parse. The neighbor’s cat, a shadow in the bushes, seems to know something has shifted, a balance tipped. The wind rustles the leaves, a soft, shushing sound, as if nature itself is hushing the pain, telling me to be still, to let it pass.

But it doesn’t. It lingers, a weight in my chest, a stone in the river of time. I walk the paths we once shared, the leash in my hand a phantom limb, a reminder of the warmth and the pull. The park bench, our favorite spot, is now just wood and metal, a place for strangers to rest, not a throne for a king and his loyal subject.

At night, I listen for your breath, the gentle rise and fall, a lullaby that never came. The darkness is a heavy blanket, and I am cold, a solitary figure in a bed too big for one. I reach out, half-expecting to feel the soft fur, the thump-thump of your heart, but there is only the cool, empty air, a void where you used to be.

And so, I carry you with me, a silent, invisible presence, a shadow at my side. In the spaces between the moments, in the pauses of the day, I see you, a flicker, a memory, a ghost. And though the world moves on, a relentless march, I hold onto the fragments, the pieces of you, a mosaic of love and loss, a testament to the dog who was, and will always be, a part of me.

title: dramatic monologue|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The Orchard’s Fourfold Tongue  

I am the orchard—rooted, raw, and old—  
and I have spoken in four tongues of time:  

First, *Spring*: a shiver in the bone-deep dark,  
a green fist punching through the frost’s grey shroud.  
Buds swell like unspoken vows—tight, pale, trembling—  
then burst: a riot of pink and white, a blinding shout  
that drowns the wind in perfume thick as prayer.  
Bees drone hymns; branches bow beneath their own bright weight—  
but I feel it then—the first thin thread of loss,  
how every bloom is already counting down to fall.  

Then *Summer*: heavy, hushed, and honey-slow.  
Leaves grow broad and dark, a canopy of green fire.  
Fruit swells—hard, green, secretive—deep in the shade,  
each one a secret turning, tight and tart,  
while sun stitches gold into their skin.  
I hold them all—this slow, sweet, swelling ache—  
but feel the soil grow thirsty, the sky grow thin,  
and hear the rustle—not of wind—but of wings  
gathering, waiting, in the heat’s low hum.  

Then *Autumn*: the reckoning. A sudden hush.  
Leaves ignite—crimson, amber, bruised gold—  
then let go, spiraling in silent, slow surrender.  
Apples drop—thud, thud, thud—like muffled drums  
on moss and loam. Some split, some rot, some roll  
into the ditch where foxes come to feast.  
I stand stripped, stark—a latticework of bone—  
every branch a question mark against the grey.  
This is not death—not yet—but the long exhale,  
the letting go that tastes like cider, sharp and sweet,  
and sorrow worn like a well-fitted glove.  

Then *Winter*: the silence that has teeth.  
Snow falls—not soft, but sharp, like shattered glass—  
and settles on the boughs, a brittle, blinding shroud.  
No leaf. No fruit. No bird. Only the wind’s cold tongue  
licking at the bark, carving names no one will read.  
My roots grip deep—black, knotted, patient—  
holding the memory of sap, of blossom, of weight.  
I am not empty. I am *holding*.  
Holding the ghost of green. The echo of bees.  
The map of every branch, drawn in ice and starlight.  
This is my oldest voice: not lament, not hope—  
but the deep, slow grammar of endurance:  
*Wait. Remember. Break. Begin again.*  
I am the orchard.  
I am the turning.  
I am the ground where all four seasons kneel.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the first heartbreak
text:
Sonnet: The First Heartbreak  

That April dawn, when cherry boughs hung low  
With blossoms trembling in the misted air,  
You stood beside the fountain’s marble flow—  
Your laughter light, your presence bright and fair.  
I thought love was a sun that would not fade,  
A vow as sure as oak or ancient stone;  
I traced the map of promises we made,  
Each word a seed I’d tenderly have sown.  

Then came the letter—ink still sharp and cold—  
A single page, unsealed, left on my desk;  
No tear, no tremor in the script, but bold  
And final as a gravestone’s stark request.  
The world went silent. Petals dropped like rain.  
My heart, unpracticed, broke—and learned its pain.

title: dramatic monologue|watching a parent grow old
text:
Whispers of the Past

In the quiet corners of our home, you sit,  
A silhouette against the fading light,  
Your hands, once strong, now tremble with each fit,  
And in your eyes, I see the shadows of the night.  

The Unspoken Words

How do I tell you that I fear the dark?  
That every slow step, every pause, it breaks my heart?  
Words stick in my throat, a heavy, silent stone,  
While time, relentless, carves its lines, and we are left alone.  

Echoes of Tomorrow

Now, as dawn breaks, I watch you from afar,  
In every line, every crease, I see a map of stars,  
Guiding me through this journey, both sweet and sore,  
Together, we walk, into the gentle, golden door.

title: short lyric poem|the night shift at a diner
text:
Night Shift at the Neon Diner

Coffee steams in chipped white mugs,  
clock hands drag like tired feet—  
the grill hisses low, a steady hum,  
while city lights blink, incomplete.  

A trucker leans on vinyl, eyes half-lidded,  
a nurse traces steam on cold glass,  
a student under fluorescent glare  
counts change and watches minutes pass.  

The jukebox sighs a slow old tune,  
the fryer bubbles, gold and deep,  
and somewhere past the saltshaker’s rim,  
the world forgets to sleep.  

We pour the dark like syrup thick,  
wipe counters clean of ghosts and grime—  
not heroes, not saints, just keepers of light  
in the long, soft hush between time.

title: villanelle|a mother's hands
text:
Mother’s Hands

Not soft as dough, but knuckled, veined, and thin—  
a map of rivers dried to cracked clay beds—  
they stitch the world back when the world gives in.  

I watched them split the stubborn winter skin  
of squash, press garlic through the rusted grater’s teeth—  
not soft as dough, but knuckled, veined, and thin.  

They held my wrist when fever burned within,  
palm cool as river stone against my brow’s hot ledge—  
they stitch the world back when the world gives in.  

Once, they gripped a wrench, elbow-deep in grime,  
fixed the porch swing’s hinge with grease-blackened grace—  
not soft as dough, but knuckled, veined, and thin.  

They wiped chalk-dust from my third-grade slate, then skimmed  
the grease off broth with a spoon’s quick, silver sweep—  
they stitch the world back when the world gives in.  

Now, one trembles mid-air, a moth against the light,  
the other rests, palm-up, on the quilt’s worn edge—  
not soft as dough, but knuckled, veined, and thin.  
They stitch the world back when the world gives in.

title: prose poem|an old piano left on the curb
text:
An Old Piano Left on the Curb

Beneath the weeping willow's tender shade,  
A relic of melodies past now waits,  
Its keys like whispers from a bygone age,  
Each one a story that time erases.

The streetlights flicker, casting gentle beams,  
Over its polished wood, now marred with dreams.  
Here once danced notes, in joy and sorrow dressed,  
Now silent, save for the wind's soft caress.

Children pass, their eyes wide with wonder,  
Tapping lightly, as if to awaken slumber.  
But the piano, patient, holds its breath,  
Knowing well the dance of life and death.

Night falls, stars twinkle in the velvet sky,  
And still it sits, under moonlight's sigh.  
An old piano left on the curb, alone,  
Guarding secrets of a forgotten tone.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|learning a second language as an adult
text:
My tongue, that knew but English since my birth,  
Now stumbles o’er the *r* in *carrefour*—  
A guttural scrape, like dragging rusted earth,  
While native speakers laugh and say, “Not *there*, sir!”  
I bought a phrasebook in a Lyon stall,  
Its pages warped from rain and coffee spills;  
I traced the verbs with trembling, ink-stained thumb,  
And whispered *je voudrais* to empty hills.  
Last Tuesday, I ordered croissants—*trois*, not *trois*—  
The baker paused, then slid me four instead,  
His eyebrow arched, a silent, kind rebuke.  
My notebook’s full of crossings-out, half-read,  
With stars beside *ser*/*estar*, and notes:  
*“Ask Maria how her cat’s new kittens are.”*

title: ode|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
I. The Abandonment  
A single glove, grey wool gone stiff with rain,  
Clings to the splintered post like a tired hand—  
Fingers curled as if still grasping air,  
Thumb hooked on rust, refusing land.  
No owner returns. No wind unfastens it.  
It watches the road, mute and half-unbuttoned.

II. The Witnessing  
Dawn gilds its knuckles; noon bleaches the seam.  
Sparrows inspect its hollow, call it strange.  
Frost stitches silver along each ridge,  
Then thaw unravels what the cold had chained.  
It holds the shape of absence, taut and thin—  
A vessel filled with light, not skin, not kin.

III. The Unfurling  
One gust—a sigh—the cuff lets go at last.  
It lifts, a small grey wing, then dips, then spins,  
Tangling once in thistle, caught mid-flight,  
Before the current wins and carries it—  
Not home, not lost, but loosened from the post,  
A breath released where memory wears thin.

title: ghazal|a mother's hands
text:
Title: The Weaver's Grace

In her hands, the threads of life and lore are spun,  
A mother's touch, where warmth and wisdom run.

Through years that pass like whispers in the night,  
Her palms, a cradle soft, a guiding light.

They mend the tears with stitches fine and neat,  
And in their lines, love’s tender map is sweet.

These hands that shaped our world with gentle art,  
Are time’s own canvas, bearing every part.

Yet ask not what these weary hands have gained,  
For in their work, no effort was in vain.

title: ghazal|the night shift at a diner
text:
The coffee urn glows like a fallen streetlamp’s eye,  
steam rising—not prayer—but the ghost of last night’s fry.  

My apron holds lint, a fossilized crumb of rye toast,  
and the sugar shaker’s hollow chime when I tilt it dry.  

The clock above the grill ticks in reverse—just once—  
then settles, its hands fused at 3:17, a lie.  

A trucker unzips his jacket; cold air spills out,  
carrying pine resin and the static of a dead CB mic.  

The cherry pie slice trembles on its plate—jellied light,  
not red, but the bruised purple of a thumbprint left behind.  

I wipe the same counter groove where a ring left its mark,  
a silver scar no bleach can lift, no rag can deny.  

You ask for “the usual”—but your usual changed last Tuesday,  
when you stopped ordering eggs and started staring at the sky.  

The neon “OPEN” buzzes, a trapped wasp against the glass,  
its hum the only thing that knows the hour is true.  

I pour black coffee into cups already warm from ghosts,  
and the steam doesn’t rise—it *unfurls*, slow, thin, and blue.

title: blank verse meditation|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
Dawn’s First Cup  

The world is still—a breath held in the dark,  
A hush so deep the ceiling fan’s low hum  
Sounds like a distant tide against the shore.  
Outside, the sky bleeds gray into soft rose,  
While streetlights blink their last, reluctant gold.  
I sit alone, wrapped in the quiet’s weight,  
The kitchen warm with steam and bitter scent—  
Rich, earthy, sharp—the first true note of day.  

The mug is warm beneath my palms, its curve  
Familiar as an old friend’s steady hand.  
I watch the surface tremble, thin and black,  
A mirror holding back the coming light.  
No voices rise, no footsteps cross the floor,  
No phone’s insistent chime, no urgent call—  
Just this: the slow descent of steam, the grind  
Of memory turning in the silent air.  

The coffee cools—not yet too cool to drink—  
A small surrender to the body’s need,  
To warmth, to wakefulness, to what is real  
Before the world reclaims its noise and names.  
I sip, and taste the dark before the dawn,  
The pause between what was and what will be—  
Not emptiness, but fullness held in wait,  
A vessel filled, not with what’s asked, but given:  
This hour, this heat, this breath, this cup, this calm.

title: dramatic monologue|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
These feet, they drag like anchors through the halls,
Twelve hours, and the world's a blur of walls.
My back, a map of aches, each step a story,
Ninety-six floors walked, or so they say in glory.

The smell of antiseptic, it clings to me,
A second skin, as close as can be.
I've seen the faces, young and old,
Held hands that trembled, told tales untold.

There was Mrs. Green, with her faded eyes,
Whispering secrets of yesteryears' lies.
And little Timmy, his leg in a cast,
Promised me he’d run again, fast and fast.

I’ve mopped up tears, held ice chips to lips,
Changed sheets stained with sweat, and whispered soft quips.
But tonight, the weight is just too much,
Too many ghosts, too many touches.

The clock ticks slow, the night drags on,
I count the minutes, till I am gone.
Outside, the world sleeps, dreams in peace,
While I, a soldier, in this endless crease.

My badge, it gleams, a medal of sorts,
A name tag worn, by tired, weary forts.
I’ll head home now, to an empty bed,
Where sleep eludes, and thoughts tread.

Tomorrow, I’ll return, to do it all again,
To mend and heal, to fight the pain.
But for now, I’ll let the darkness take,
This weary soul, for its own sake.

title: blank verse meditation|an old piano left on the curb
text:
Curb Piano  

The rain has stopped. A slant of afternoon light  
catches the dust motes swirling above its lid—  
a cracked veneer, like dry riverbeds,  
where walnut grain once held a deeper gloss.  
Its bench lies askew, one leg snapped clean,  
a splintered hinge still clinging to the frame.  
Keys yellow as old parchment, brittle at the edges;  
middle C chipped, a small white crater  
where a child’s thumb pressed, long ago.  

No bench to sit on now—just damp concrete,  
a plastic bag snagged on the sustain pedal,  
fluttering like a trapped bird’s last wingbeat.  
I kneel—not to play, but to listen:  
the hollow hum inside the soundboard,  
the slow surrender of felt to moth,  
the faint metallic sigh of rust blooming  
in the harp’s cold, exposed strings.  

Someone left it here. Not broken beyond repair,  
but *unwanted*—a vessel emptied of use,  
yet still holding resonance in its ribs,  
still shaped by decades of breath and weight,  
of lullabies, arguments, late-night fugues,  
of fingers trembling before first recitals.  
It does not beg. It does not mourn.  
It simply *is*: wood, wire, silence thick as velvet,  
waiting—not for rescue, but for witness.  

I rise. The streetlamp flickers on,  
casting its long, thin shadow across the keys—  
a ghostly staff, no notes written yet.  
And for a breath, the air itself seems tuned,  
vibrating just below hearing—  
as if the world, for all its haste,  
had paused to hold one sustained, unplayed chord.

title: spoken-word poem|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Lunar Witness  

She rises—  
not silver, not serene—  
but a cracked plate of bone-white light  
spilling over barbed wire,  
over tents stitched from torn plastic and prayer,  
over children who count stars like lost names.  

She watches the mother kneel in dust,  
stirring lentils in a dented pot,  
her wrist thin as a reed,  
her shadow long and trembling—  
a second refugee, cast by the same cold eye.  

She sees the boy who draws craters in the sand  
with a stick, calls them *home*,  
though his home has no moon—  
only smoke, only sirens,  
only the hollow echo of a door that won’t open again.  

She hears the old man whisper to the sky:  
*You were there when my orchard bloomed.  
You were there when the bombs fell like hail.  
You are here now—  
but you do not speak.  
You do not choose sides.  
You only hold the dark,  
and let us hold it too.*  

Oh, she is ancient.  
She has seen empires burn and bloom like desert flowers.  
She has watched borders shift like dunes,  
watched maps redrawn in blood and ink.  
She does not mourn.  
She does not rage.  
She simply *is*—  
a silent covenant,  
a shared breath between exile and earth,  
between what was taken  
and what still rises,  
still glows,  
still pulls the tides in the throat of the displaced,  
still says, without words:  
*You are seen.  
You are held.  
You are not alone beneath this borrowed light.*  

So tonight—  
when the wind lifts the flaps of the tent,  
when the guard’s flashlight sweeps the perimeter,  
when someone hums a lullaby in a language the moon remembers—  
look up.  
She is not refuge.  
She is not rescue.  
But she is witness.  
And sometimes,  
that is the first, fragile shape of grace.

title: villanelle|moving out of a childhood home
text:
In rooms where echoes of my laughter cling,
I box the stars that once adorned the walls.
The house, a silent book, its pages fling.

Each drawer a chest where secret dreams took flight,
Now emptied, like the nest before the fall.
In rooms where echoes of my laughter cling,

The kitchen tiles, a map of spilled sauces,
Mark journeys to and from, in endless calls.
The house, a silent book, its pages fling.

A chipped mug holds the ghost of morning brews,
Its handle warm with hands that now appall.
In rooms where echoes of my laughter cling,

The garden's wild, as if it knew I’d go,
Its weeds reclaim the paths, a green enthrall.
The house, a silent book, its pages fling.

At last, the key turns, heavy in my palm,
A lock clicks, sealing all the years in thrall.
In rooms where echoes of my laughter cling,
The house, a silent book, its pages fling.

title: ode|a soldier writing home
text:
Ode to the Unsent Letter  

Dear Mother,  
The ink bleeds faint on this thin, gray sheet—  
Not from my hand’s unsteady press,  
But from the rain that drums the trench’s teeth,  
And the slow seep of dusk through ragged wool.  
I write by candle-glow too weak to hold  
The shape of home: your kitchen door ajar,  
The kettle’s low hum, steam like prayer rising—  
All blurred now, as if seen through salt-stung glass.  

I tell you the ground is hard, but not too hard;  
The bread is coarse, but fills the hollow place;  
The lark still sings at dawn above the wire—  
A small, bright treason against all this steel.  
I do not tell you how the silence after shells  
Is louder than the blast; how names dissolve  
Like sugar in the canteen’s bitter tea;  
How I trace your initials in the dust each night  
And wipe them quick before the next patrol.  

This letter will not fly—it lacks the stamp,  
The proper weight, the courage to be sent.  
It lives instead inside my breast-pocket,  
Where warmth and worry share the same small space—  
A folded map of all I cannot say,  
And all I am too tender to unmake.  
So let it stay: a quiet, constant vow—  
Not lost, but held, until the war lets go.

title: ode|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
October 12th, 3:47 p.m.  
The light’s that thin, brittle gold—  
like the foil wrapper off a cough drop  
I found wedged in my coat pocket last week,  
still faintly minty, still crumpled.  

Maple leaves, mostly.  
Not the showy reds—the ones that scream.  
These are the tired ones:  
russet, burnt umber, the colour of old tea stains  
on my mother’s best saucer, the one with the hairline crack  
she kept using anyway.  

They cling to the iron fence—  
not stuck, not clinging, just… paused—  
as if they’d meant to fall but changed their minds  
mid-air, like I did  
that Tuesday I walked past the florist  
and didn’t buy the chrysanthemums  
for Eleanor’s stone.  
Too expensive. Too pink.  
Too much like the plastic ones  
they put on the casket at Dad’s service—  
the kind that don’t wilt, don’t fade,  
don’t smell like anything real.  

One leaf, damp and veined like a thumbnail,  
stuck to the base of the Hargrove headstone—  
1928–1999.  
No epitaph. Just the name,  
and a tiny, lopsided dove carved by someone  
whose hands shook a little, or maybe just hurried.  
The leaf trembles when the wind lifts—  
not enough to fly, not enough to let go.  

I kicked a pile near the willow oak.  
Mud-slicked, sour-sweet rot,  
a whiff of wet dog and forgotten apples.  
My boot sank a little.  
Left a print.  
Then the wind took three of them—  
not up, not down—just sideways,  
tangling in the bare stems of the forsythia  
that hasn’t bloomed here in seven years.  

I didn’t stay.  
Just zipped my coat higher,  
felt the frayed thread inside the cuff catch on my wrist,  
and walked back toward the gate,  
leaving the leaves where they were—  
some stuck, some sliding,  
some already buried under what’s coming next.

title: ode|drought on a family farm
text:
Beneath the sun's relentless gaze, our fields lie still,
A canvas of despair, where hope once danced and thrilled.
The earth, a cracked and weary face, begs for rain's sweet kiss,
Each fissure telling tales of thirst, in silent, solemn hiss.

Our barn stands like a ghost, its timbers dry and worn,
Its shadows stretch across the land, a sight both bleak and torn.
The well, a mouth agape, no longer sings its song,
Its depths, a hollow echo, where water used to throng.

The river, once a lifeline, meanders slow and thin,
Its banks, a graveyard for dreams, beneath the ashen skin.
The cattle, with their mournful eyes, roam in search of green,
Their hooves stir up the dust, a dance so sad, so lean.

My father, strong and stoic, surveys this desolate scene,
His hands, once sure and steady, now tremble, seldom seen.
He speaks of rains to come, of clouds that will appear,
But in his voice, a quiver, a hint of gathering fear.

At night, we gather 'round, our hearts heavy with dread,
The stars, like distant promises, cold and overhead.
We pray for mercy, for a drop, a sign, a gentle fall,
To bring back life, to heal the wounds, to answer nature's call.

Yet, in the quiet moments, when despair threatens to claim,
We find a strength within us, a flame that still remains.
For though the drought may test us, and strip away our yield,
It cannot break the spirit, nor steal the love we feel.

title: elegy|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. The Threshold  
The door sighs open—cinnamon and yeast,  
a warm breath rising from the oven’s throat.  
Flour dust hangs like suspended time,  
and sugar glistens on her knuckles, soft and slow.  
I step in, and the air remembers me  
before I do.  

II. The Simmer  
Onions weep in golden pools of butter,  
cloves bloom sharp beneath the steam of stew.  
Her apron bears the ghosts of vanilla,  
of burnt sugar, of yesterday’s bread.  
She stirs without looking—her wrist a compass—  
and the pot hums low, a lullaby in broth.  

III. The Absence  
Now the stove is cold, the cupboard still.  
A single bay leaf crumbles in an empty jar.  
I press my nose to the faded checkered cloth—  
faintest trace of nutmeg, ghost of smoke,  
the hollow where her warmth once lived and breathed—  
and the kitchen holds its breath, waiting for a hand  
that will never lift the wooden spoon again.

title: blank verse meditation|the night shift at a diner
text:
The coffee urn exhales its sour steam—  
not mist, but a slow, greasy sigh that clings  
to the chrome edge of the counter like old gum.  
My apron’s stiff with dried syrup and bleach,  
a second skin stitched with salt and burnt sugar.  

At 2:47, the fryer gurgles—not bubbles,  
but something deeper: a wet, guttural churn,  
like gravel shifting in a drowned throat.  
A trucker slams his palm on Formica—  
not for service, just to hear the hollow *thunk*  
that vibrates up through his knuckles, into his molars.  

The neon “OPEN” sign flickers—not strobes,  
but a stutter: *O—pen—O—pen—*,  
as if the letters are forgetting their own names.  
Outside, rain doesn’t fall; it *sheds*—  
thin silver scales peeling off the black sky,  
glinting once on the hood of a dented Camry  
before dissolving into the gutter’s slow, oily tongue.  

I scrape cold hash browns from a plate—  
they don’t crumble. They *unspool*,  
pale ribbons curling at the edges,  
still holding the ghost-heat of the griddle.  
My wrist aches—not sharp, but dull,  
like a hinge slowly filling with rust-sand.  

A woman in a parka lined with fake fur  
orders black coffee, no cup, no lid—  
just holds the mug upright, palms cupped beneath,  
letting the heat rise, unspent, into her wrists.  
She doesn’t drink. She lets the steam write  
tiny, vanishing maps on her lower lip.  

The clock above the fry station doesn’t tick.  
It *blinks*: a red LED, patient, indifferent,  
counting seconds not as time, but as weight—  
each one settling, grain by grain,  
into the hollow behind my collarbone.  

Dawn won’t arrive with light.  
It’ll come as a thinning—  
a graying of the window’s black glass,  
then the slow, reluctant lift  
of the city’s exhaust-haze,  
like a sheet pulled back from something breathing,  
but not yet awake.

title: ballad in quatrains|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
A Lost Glove on a Fence Post

Upon a post, a glove did rest,  
Beneath the moon's soft silver glow,  
Alone it lay, as if to attest,  
To stories only night winds know.

Its mate was gone, in fields afar,  
Or maybe lost within the town,  
This single glove, beneath a star,  
Wore solitude like a crown.

The fence, a line 'twixt field and sky,  
Held secrets of the silent land,  
While shadows danced, and time went by,  
The glove upon its perch did stand.

Who left it there, no one can say,  
Perhaps a traveler in haste,  
Now seasons change, from day to day,  
Yet still the glove retains its grace.

title: ballad in quatrains|an old piano left on the curb
text:
It sat there Tuesday, rain-slick and thin,  
keys yellowed like old cigarette packs,  
one leg propped on a soggy cardboard box—  
the kind you get from U-Haul, taped with black duct.  

I recognized the brand: Kimball, ’73.  
My cousin Lenny played “Für Elise” on one just like it,  
fingers stubby, knuckles red from scrubbing floors,  
before he vanished down I-95 with a duffel and three quarters.  

The middle C stuck—always did—  
a sour note that hummed when trucks rumbled past.  
A coffee ring bloomed under the music rest,  
and someone had carved *M + J* deep in the left cheek,  
then scratched it out halfway, leaving ghost-letters.  

Mrs. Gable from 4B tried to play “Silent Night”  
on Christmas Eve, 2018,  
but her wrist gave out mid-verse,  
and the last chord hung, unbalanced,  
like a question no one answered.  

I walked by it six times.  
Took a photo. Didn’t post it.  
Left my gloves on the bench beside it—  
wool, gray, one thumbhole frayed raw.  

The city truck came Thursday.  
They tipped it sideways, and a moth flew out  
from between the bass strings,  
wings dusted with something that looked like chalk,  
or maybe just old piano wire rust.

title: poem in tercets|a soldier writing home
text:
Letter from the Trenches  

The candle gutters—wax like frozen tears—  
I trace your name in ink that blurs and bleeds,  
While rats gnaw silence at the foot of years.  

My fingers tremble—not from cold, but need:  
This paper’s thin as hope, this envelope  
A fragile raft on waters choked with lead.  

Outside, the sky is stitched with shrapnel’s thread,  
A jagged seam where stars refuse to rise;  
Inside, your photograph—a sun instead—  
Warm light pooled in my palm, soft as a sigh.  

I write you lilacs (though no lilacs bloom here),  
Describe the lark that sang above the wire—  
A silver stitch in air, so brief, so clear—  
Then tear the page. You must not know the mire.  

So I sign *All well*, though mud has claimed my boots,  
Though every breath tastes iron, salt, and smoke,  
And love is just this trembling, ink-stained truth:  
I hold you close by what I do not spoke.

title: dramatic monologue|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
Whispers of the Tide

In shallow whispers, the tide calls out,
Beneath the moon’s soft, silver rout.
Pools cradle secrets in their brine,
Where hermit crabs in shells do shine.

 The Hermit's Dance

I scuttle through the cool, wet sand,
A borrowed home, a secondhand.
My shell, a fortress, strong and true,
In this small world, I find my crew.

 Echoes of the Sea

When waves retreat, we linger still,
In tiny pools, our hearts to fill.
The sea’s embrace, a distant dream,
Yet here, in quiet, we gleam.

title: free verse poem|the sound of a train at night
text:
Night Train’s Throat  

A low hum first—  
not heard, but felt:  
a tremor in the floorboard,  
a shiver in the teacup’s rim.  

Then the groan—  
metal stretching its spine,  
wheels grinding memory into gravel,  
a slow, insistent *shhh-shhh-shhh*  
like breath drawn through dry reeds.  

Distant, a whistle cuts—  
not sharp, but hollow,  
a note pulled thin across fields,  
unspooling into the dark like smoke  
that doesn’t rise, but *settles*.  

Closer now:  
the clack-clack-clack—  
rhythmic, weary, inevitable—  
each joint in the track sighing  
as the weight passes,  
as if the earth itself  
were counting seconds  
between heartbeats.  

Then the rush—  
a wind that isn’t wind,  
a roar that swallows crickets,  
a sudden heat and iron scent  
rushing past the window—  
a black river of light and shadow,  
streaked with yellow eyes,  
gone before the echo finishes  
its long, slow fade.  

Silence returns—  
but softer now,  
thrumming with after-sound,  
holding the shape of motion  
in the still air,  
in the quiet walls,  
in the pulse behind your ears—  
as if the night,  
for one breath,  
had borrowed the train’s rhythm  
and forgotten to give it back.

title: blank verse meditation|teenage summer jobs
text:
Summer Shifts  

The sun climbs sharp above the parking lot,  
a furnace lid held open by the noon.  
I mop the floor where soda spills have dried  
to sticky constellations—brown and thin—  
and smell the bleach that stings my throat and eyes.  
My sneakers squeak on wet linoleum,  
a sound like small birds trapped inside the walls.  
Outside, the world is all cicadas, heat,  
and bicycles that vanish down the street  
with backpacks flapping like untrained wings.  

At three, the register chimes its thin song:  
*beep—beep—beep*—as coins clink cold and heavy  
into my palm, a weight I don’t yet trust.  
Mrs. Delaney buys her weekly chips,  
her smile a practiced curve above her mask;  
the boy from soccer nods but won’t make eye contact—  
just grabs his Slurpee, frost already weeping  
down the red plastic cup. I count the hours  
not in minutes, but in paper cups stacked,  
in napkin rolls unwound, in receipts curled  
like sleeping snakes beside the cash drawer’s hum.  

Sometimes, behind the cooler’s glass, I pause—  
watch condensation bloom and blur the light—  
and wonder if this ache behind my knees,  
this quiet burn behind my temples, means  
I’m building something real, or just enduring  
the long, slow grammar of becoming:  
how work teaches the body its own limits,  
how boredom carves its subtle, steady lines,  
how dignity hides not in the title,  
but in showing up—still damp, still tired,  
still wiping up what someone else has spilled.

title: elegy|a beekeeper in winter
text:
In the hush of winter, under a sky so pale,
He tended to his silent hives, where bees once flailed.
His hands, rough as the bark of ancient trees,
Now felt the cold, unyielding air, and whispered to the breeze.

The world was still, save for the creak of old bones,
And the distant murmur of the river, like a mournful tone.
His coat, patched with memories, hung heavy on his frame,
A tapestry of summers past, now wrapped in frosty shame.

The fields lay bare, stripped of their golden bounty,
Where he once walked, a king among the honeyed plenty.
But now, the flowers were ghosts, their colors bled away,
Leaving only the stark, unforgiving gray.

He spoke to them, those empty hives, in a voice so low,
As if the bees could hear him, though they’d long since flown.
“Rest well, my darlings, till the sun returns to warm your wings,
Till spring’s sweet promise brings you back, and life again it brings.”

The snow fell softly, a shroud upon the earth,
And he stood there, a sentinel, guarding what was left of mirth.
His heart, a quiet ache, beat slow beneath his chest,
A testament to love, and loss, and all that time had pressed.

title: sequence of haiku|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Moon Over the Camp  

Barren ground—  
a child’s tin cup catches  
cold light.  

Tent ropes hum  
with wind from the border hills—  
moon, unblinking.  

One blanket, two shoulders,  
the same silver on dust  
and eyelashes.

title: ghazal|watching a parent grow old
text:
I. Trembling Hands  
Your hands, once steady as a compass rose,  
now tremble—like leaves in a wind that no one knows.  
You fumble the teacup, spill what’s warm and known,  
while time pours through your fingers like sifted snows.  
I reach to hold them, but you pull away—  
a gesture learned from years of bearing loads.  
The map of veins has risen, thin and blue,  
a river charting where the current slows.  
You smile: *It’s nothing.* I nod: *Of course it’s not.*  
Two lies we keep, like vows we’ve softly sewn.  

II. Fading Names  
You pause mid-sentence, brow drawn tight and thin,  
searching the air for names you used to own.  
A neighbor’s face—a ghost behind the glass—  
you call her “Eleanor,” though she’s long since gone.  
The photo album lies open on your lap:  
a boy in shorts, a dog with sunlit nose.  
You trace his cheek and whisper, *Who is this?*  
as if the past were written in vanishing prose.  
I name him—your brother, gone at twenty-two—  
and watch your eyes go quiet, soft, and slow.  

III. Light Through the Window  
You sit where morning light still finds its way,  
a pool of gold across the worn oak floor.  
Your breathing deepens—not quite sleep, not wake—  
a tide receding past the silent shore.  
I kneel beside you, brush a strand aside,  
and feel the fragile architecture of your bone.  
No grand farewell, no final, burning word—  
just this: the light, the hush, the love, the bone.  
The room holds still. The world outside moves on.  
And in your palm, my hand feels strangely small—  
not holding on, but learning how to let go,  
soft as dust settling on a sunlit wall.

title: free verse poem|time and memory
text:
Whispers of the Clock

In the quiet corners of forgotten rooms,
Time tiptoes, leaving no footprints, only echoes.
Each tick, a heartbeat of the universe,
Pulsing through corridors of our yesterdays.

Memories, like autumn leaves, scatter
Across the landscape of our minds,
Some golden, crisp, and cherished,
Others, faded, brittle, lost to the winds.

We hold onto moments, fragile as glass,
Fearing the shatter, the final letting go.
Yet, in each fragment lies a story,
A whispered secret of who we once were.

Time is a river, flowing, ever-changing,
Carving canyons deep within our souls.
And though its current pulls us forward,
Our reflections linger in the still waters behind.

title: ode|grief after a dog dies
text:
Ode to the Hollow Where the Dog Was

Not the collar left on the hook—  
too neat, too tidy, a prop.  

Not the silence where barks used to ricochet off the garage door—  
silence is lazy; grief is louder.  

It’s the way the floorboards remember the weight:  
a dent near the radiator, faint as a bruise,  
where she’d sink each afternoon,  
paws splayed like spilled ink,  
nose resting on the cool tile  
like a dropped spoon.  

It’s the grocery bag I carried in  
still smelling of wet fur and kibble dust—  
not sadness, but *absence with scent*,  
a chemical ghost clinging to the plastic.  

It’s the way the leash hangs now:  
not coiled, not knotted—  
just slack, a dead rope  
draped over the banister,  
its metal clasp cold,  
unblinking,  
refusing to click open.  

It’s the coffee mug I rinsed twice this morning  
because the rim held one stray black hair—  
not sentimental, just *evidence*,  
a filament of biology  
that shouldn’t still be there.  

It’s the way the neighbor’s terrier barks at 4:17 p.m.,  
and my hand twitches—  
not toward the door,  
but toward the empty space beside the couch,  
where her shoulder used to press warm  
against my thigh,  
a living brace.  

Grief isn’t a stone in the chest.  
It’s the thermostat set wrong for weeks—  
I keep turning it down,  
forgetting the heat wasn’t hers,  
but the *lack* of her warmth  
has rewired the air.  

And tonight,  
the vacuum hums in the hall,  
and for half a second,  
I hear the rustle of her ears  
flicking at the sound—  
not memory, but muscle:  
my jaw tightens,  
my shoulders lift—  
the body rehearsing a response  
to a presence that’s gone  
but hasn’t yet untaught the nerves.  

That’s the hollow.  
Not an echo.  
A physics problem:  
mass removed,  
field still trembling.

title: blank verse meditation|the first heartbreak
text:
I remember the exact shade of that blue sweater—  
not navy, not denim, but the faded kind  
you get from washing it too many times  
in hot water, then hanging it outside  
where the sun bleaches the collar unevenly.  
You wore it the day you said, *I’m not sure  
I want to keep doing this*, and I nodded  
like I understood, like I’d read the fine print  
on the back of your throat when you swallowed.  

My hands were cold even though it was May.  
I stood in your kitchen, leaning against  
the chipped Formica counter, watching steam  
rise from your mug—peppermint tea, always  
peppermint, even in summer—and thinking  
how strange it is that grief doesn’t roar,  
but hums: a low, persistent fridge-thrum  
behind the walls of your own ribs.  

Later, walking home past the laundromat  
where we’d once shared quarters and silence,  
I dropped my keys twice. Not dramatic—just  
a dull clatter on wet pavement, then again  
three blocks on, like my fingers forgot  
how to hold anything. My left sock had a hole  
near the big toe. I noticed it only  
because I kept staring at my feet,  
as if they might betray me next.  

The worst part wasn’t crying. It was  
the way my voice stayed steady on the phone  
with my mother, describing the weather,  
the bus schedule, the price of avocados—  
all perfectly ordinary things,  
all perfectly true,  
all perfectly hollow.

title: sequence of haiku|a beekeeper in winter
text:
Snow muffles the hives,  
Silent bees in winter's hold—  
Keeper's breath turns white.

Empty gloves hang still,  
Smoke cools in the crisp air, waits—  
Spring's distant promise.

Sunset paints the snow,  
Golden light on silent frames—  
Hope warms his old hands.

title: sequence of haiku|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Neon Threshold  
Rain slicks the sidewalk—  
blue light bleeds on wet pavement.  
Door swings, warm breath spills.  

Midnight Set  
Saxophone sighs—  
rain taps time on the windowpane.  
Smoke curls, slow and low.  

Last Call Drizzle  
Empty glasses gleam.  
Umbrellas bloom like dark flowers—  
rain hums the same tune.

title: ballad in quatrains|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
First Gear

The keys were cold within her palm,  
Her knuckles white, her breath held tight,  
He sat beside her, calm and warm,  
Beneath the pale and patient light.  

“Left foot down—now ease it up,”  
Her engine coughed, then stalled, then sighed.  
He didn’t scold, he didn’t rush—  
Just smiled and said, “We’ll try again, my guide.”  

The clutch slipped once, the car lurched low,  
She gripped the wheel and blinked away the sting.  
He placed his hand upon her knee—  
A steady weight, a quiet, grounding thing.  

Past oak-lined streets and stop signs tall,  
She found the rhythm, slow and sure.  
He watched the road—and watched her all—  
His pride a soft, unspoken cure.  

No trophy gleamed, no medal shone,  
Just asphalt humming, sunlit air—  
Two hands on one wheel, side by side,  
And love that learned to drive with care.

title: free verse poem|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
In the neon hum of the hospital’s underbelly,  
she sheds her scrubs like a second skin,  
the fabric heavy with the day's weight—  
a tapestry of antiseptic and adrenaline.

Her feet, two stones in worn clogs,  
echo down the linoleum, a quiet drumbeat,  
each step a story: the old man who mistook her for his daughter,  
the child who drew a smiley face on her glove.

She passes the vending machine, its glass eyes  
glowing, a silent sentinel. Inside,  
chips and chocolate bars, a galaxy of salt and sugar,  
but she craves only the cool night air,  
the taste of freedom, unfiltered.

Outside, the world is a dark canvas,  
stars pinpricks in the fabric, distant and cold.  
She breathes in, the city’s breath mingling with hers,  
a symphony of exhaust and jasmine.

Her phone buzzes, a reminder: life beyond these walls.  
A text from her sister, a photo of a cat,  
curled in a sunbeam, oblivious to the world’s ache.  
She smiles, tucks the image into her heart,  
a small light against the gathering shadows.

title: blank verse meditation|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
A Garden After the Gardener Has Died  

The gate hangs loose upon its rusted hinge,  
A sigh of iron in the morning air.  
No hand has pruned the roses—tangled, thorned,  
They climb the trellis like unbidden prayers.  
The lavender, once clipped to tidy rows,  
Now spills in purple drifts across the path,  
Its scent grown thick and sweet, almost oppressive,  
As if the earth remembers how it was tended.  

The fountain’s basin holds no water now—  
Just rain-pooled stillness, leaf-mottled and deep,  
Where dragonflies skim the surface, unaware  
That stone lips once sang with silver runoff.  
The herb bed chokes with self-sown mustard,  
Parsley gone to flower, sage gone woody,  
While mint, unchecked, invades the brickwork’s seams,  
A green insistence no one names or stops.  

I walk where he walked—boots worn thin at heel,  
His straw hat hanging, faded, on a hook—  
And feel not absence, but a quiet shift:  
The garden breathes without instruction now.  
It does not mourn. It loosens, leans, reclaims—  
Not chaos, but a slower kind of order,  
Root-deep and patient, older than his hands.  
The soil remembers every seed he sowed,  
Yet yields to what the wild wind chooses next.  
I stand beside the pear tree, heavy-limbed,  
Its fruit fallen, softening into loam—  
And understand: to tend is not to own,  
But to release—then let the light come through.

title: pantoum|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
Driving Lesson  

The clutch bites soft beneath her small, white hand,  
Sunlight pools on the dashboard, warm and thin.  
She grips the wheel like something she must understand—  
The road ahead unspools, both steep and kin.  

Sunlight pools on the dashboard, warm and thin,  
A humming silence where the engine breathes.  
The road ahead unspools, both steep and kin—  
His voice, a steady current underneath.  

A humming silence where the engine breathes,  
Her knuckles pale, her gaze fixed on the bend.  
His voice, a steady current underneath,  
One hand hovering—not holding, but *there*, friend.  

Her knuckles pale, her gaze fixed on the bend,  
Past mailboxes, a startled deer, a curve.  
One hand hovering—not holding, but *there*, friend—  
Then—suddenly—the car holds its own nerve.  

Past mailboxes, a startled deer, a curve,  
She shifts, exhales—a laugh, half-terrified.  
Then—suddenly—the car holds its own nerve—  
His pride, a quiet thing, no longer hid.  

She shifts, exhales—a laugh, half-terrified,  
The rearview mirrors catch his softened eyes:  
His pride, a quiet thing, no longer hid—  
The world expands, yet somehow, smaller, wise.  

The rearview mirrors catch his softened eyes:  
The clutch bites soft beneath her small, white hand.  
The world expands, yet somehow, smaller, wise—  
Sunlight pools on the dashboard, warm and thin.

title: prose poem|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
Silent Keeper

In the heart of silence, the garden waits,
Vines creeping like whispers over old gates.
Roses bloom in shadows, their scent a quiet plea,
For hands that once tended, now stilled by the sea.

Whispers in the Weeds

Leaves rustle with secrets, stories untold,
Of a man and his spade, now turned to cold.
The weeds grow bold, threading through the earth,
Their green fingers reaching, giving silent birth.

Eternal Bloom

Though the gardener's touch has long since fled,
His legacy lingers, in each petal, each thread.
The garden thrives, a testament to love,
A living canvas, painted from above.

title: villanelle|the sound of a train at night
text:
Night Train’s Lament

The train’s low moan cuts through the hush of night,  
A rhythmic groan on iron rails it keeps—  
It hums a tune no ear can hold or write.  

Its whistle pierces, thin and sharp and bright,  
Then fades where sleeping fields and shadows sleep,  
The train’s low moan cuts through the hush of night.  

Wheels chant a chant both ancient and uptight,  
Clack-clack-clack-clack—the world in rhythm leaps,  
It hums a tune no ear can hold or write.  

I lie awake, bathed in the pale streetlight,  
While distant crossings blink and softly beep—  
The train’s low moan cuts through the hush of night.  

Each carriage bears some unremembered plight,  
Some nameless soul who wakes and weeps and weeps—  
It hums a tune no ear can hold or write.  

No map I hold shows where its course takes flight,  
No station sign my restless heart accepts—  
The train’s low moan cuts through the hush of night,  
It hums a tune no ear can hold or write.

title: poem in tercets|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The air isn’t warm—it’s *thick*, a damp wool sock  
left in the laundry hamper, then steamed:  
cumin blooming like rust on a tin spoon.  

Not sugar, but burnt sugar—black lace  
fraying at the edge of the cooling rack,  
a bitter halo around the ginger snaps.  

Her apron smells of yeast and diesel fumes—  
she drove the ’87 Caprice to the bodega,  
still carries exhaust in the cotton weave.  

The coffee’s not rich—it’s wet newspaper  
left on the stoop overnight, then boiled down  
to a tar that coats the tongue like old varnish.  

That scent clinging to her knuckles? Not lavender,  
but the green sting of snapped celery ribs,  
and something deeper: the iron tang of thawing ground beef.  

Even the clock above the sink exhales—  
not ticking, but *dripping*: a slow leak  
from the faucet’s washer, tasting faintly of copper.

title: blank verse meditation|hope after a long illness
text:
Hope After the Long Illness

In silence, where the shadows gently fall,
And light, a fragile guest, begins to call,
There lies a quiet strength, a steady hand,
That guides the heart through night’s uncharted land.

When days of pain and struggle seem too long,
And hope, like autumn leaves, seems almost gone,
A whisper stirs, beneath the weary chest,
A gentle reminder, that time will rest.

The body, once a fortress, now worn thin,
Finds solace in the promise yet within,
For every wound, no matter deep or wide,
Is but a canvas for the soul’s own pride.

Not in the end, but in the journey’s flow,
Does truest hope and healing often grow.
Like seeds that break through earth towards the sun,
So too, the spirit, finds its way, undone.

title: ode|teenage summer jobs
text:
Ode to the Summer Jobs That Didn’t Last  

First: the Dairy Queen drive-thru, 1998—  
my voice cracking on “Would you like fries with that?”  
while Mr. Hargrove’s Buick idled, radio blaring  
some country song about a dog named Blue,  
and I’d fumble the onion rings, drop two,  
watch them skitter across the grease-slick floor  
like startled beetles. My name tag said *JEN*,  
but I’d written *JEN?* in Sharpie,  
because I wasn’t sure yet who that was.  

Then the library basement—shelving returns  
in the damp hush where light never landed,  
only the smell of mildew and old paperbacks  
with bent spines and underlined passages  
about love or revolution, both equally distant.  
I found a copy of *The Bell Jar*  
with “Maggie, 1973” written inside the cover,  
and a dried violet pressed into page 42.  
I kept it. Still have it. Not sure why.  

And the hardware store—three weeks, maybe four—  
stocking nails, sweeping sawdust,  
listening to Hank and Roy argue about carburetors  
while the ceiling fan wobbled like it might quit  
any minute, any minute, any minute.  
I wore my brother’s flannel, sleeves rolled,  
one button missing, always one button missing.  
Once, I dropped a box of 8 drywall screws  
and watched them scatter like silver ants  
across the concrete. Didn’t pick them all up.  
Just swept most into a pile, left three  
glinting near the back door, half-hidden  
by a coil of garden hose.  

No epiphany. No grand lesson.
