one’s loose. Wobbles. You can hear it hum  
if you press your ear to the metal at 2:17 a.m.,  
just before the coyotes stop barking  
and the wind forgets its own name.  

The Milky Way isn’t milk.  
It’s the residue left behind  
after scrubbing dried motor oil off a concrete floor  
with a stiff-bristled brush and too much ammonia—  
that faint, greasy, pearlescent smear  
that won’t lift, no matter how hard you scrub,  
no matter how much light you shine on it.  

And when the satellite passes?  
Not a silver thread, not a falling wish—  
it’s the slow, deliberate blink of a security camera  
mounted above a shuttered laundromat in Albuquerque,  
panning left, then pausing, then panning left again,  
recording nothing but heat-haze and dust devils  
dancing their dumb, three-second polka  
in the empty lot.  

I don’t ask the sky for meaning.  
I watch how the starlight lands  
on the cracked vinyl seat of my ’98 Corolla,  
how it pools in the shallow dent  
where my elbow rests,  
how it glints—not brightly, but *thickly*—  
off the dried coffee ring  
inside my chipped ceramic mug  
sitting cold on the hood.  

This is not awe.  
This is inventory.  
This is counting rivets,  
not constellations.  
This is knowing exactly  
how many seconds pass  
between the last cricket’s chirp  
and the first grain of sand  
shifting under my boot—  
and how, in that silence,  
the dark doesn’t deepen.  
It *settles*.  
Like sediment in a jar of well water  
you’ve stopped shaking.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a jazz club in the rain
text:
A Jazz Club in the Rain

When twilight's gentle fingers stroke the sky,
And rain, like softest whispers, starts to fall,
There lies a club where music never dies,
Its doors wide open, welcoming one and all.

The notes of saxophone, a lover's sigh,
Do mingle with the drumbeat's steady heart,
As shadows dance upon the walls nearby,
In every corner, art gives rise to art.

But lo, what magic doth the rainfall bring?
It paints the night with silver, cool, and bright,
Where lovers' eyes meet under its soft wing,
Their hearts entwined by jazz's tender light.

Though storms may rage without, within we find
A haven, warm, where love and tunes are twined.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a soldier writing home
text:
My Dearest Meg, though ink’s grown thin and blue  
(as if the sky bled through this paper’s grain),  
I write by candle—smoke stings eyes anew,  
and Private Hargrove snores like drowned-out rain.  
This mutton’s tough as boot-leather, I swear—  
yesterday I chewed a gristle for ten minutes—  
and found your last letter tucked inside my spare  
woollen sock, where damp had blurred the “kiss” you printed.  

The poppies here are thick as spilled wine, red  
but not so red as young Tom Bell’s coat-sleeve,  
torn clean at shoulder when the shrapnel sped  
past his ear—still walks, though he won’t believe  
it yet. I saved his pipe, cold and bent,  
and pressed a petal in your letter’s crease.

title: ghazal|learning a second language as an adult
text:
I. The First Word  
My tongue stumbles—foreign, thick, and slow,  
Each syllable a stone I cannot throw.  
The teacher’s voice is clear as mountain air,  
But my own mouth refuses what it knows.  
I write the script with trembling, hopeful hand,  
Yet letters blur like rain on window glass.  
This grammar feels like climbing broken stairs—  
One step up, two steps back—I still confess:  
How strange to beg for meaning, bare and new,  
When silence was my oldest, safest dress.  

II. The Lingering Ghost  
The native phrase blooms sudden in my ear—  
A scent of jasmine I once knew too near.  
My mind supplies the word I meant to say,  
Then catches—*no*, that word is not quite here.  
I dream in fragments, half in English, half  
In verbs that twist and tense without consent.  
My mother-tongue still hums beneath each line,  
A low refrain I cannot quite prevent.  
I name the world twice now—and feel unmoored,  
Like standing where two rivers intersect.  

III. The Unfolding Tongue  
Not fluency, but grace—a slower bloom,  
A quiet light dispelling old dark room.  
I speak and pause—not shame, but sacred space,  
Where listening becomes the truest room.  
The accent stays, a map of where I’ve been,  
Not flaw, but fold where self and language meet.  
One day I laugh mid-sentence, unself-conscious—  
The joke lands whole, both bitter and sweet.  
This tongue is not a copy, sharp and thin—  
It’s mine: worn, warm, and learning how to sing.

title: pantoum|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
The Distant Blaze

Smoke rises, a silent signal in the night,
From far away, the forest whispers pain.
A glow against the darkness, soft yet bright,
The trees stand witness to the fiery rain.

From far away, the forest whispers pain,
Their leaves and branches turned to ash and flame.
The trees stand witness to the fiery rain,
While shadows dance with an eerie, deadly aim.

Their leaves and branches turned to ash and flame,
A glow against the darkness, soft yet bright,
While shadows dance with an eerie, deadly aim,
Smoke rises, a silent signal in the night.

title: blank verse meditation|drought on a family farm
text:
The well’s mouth gapes—not cracked earth, but a rusted  
steel collar, cold to the knuckle, slick with dust  
that tastes like burnt toast and old batteries.  
Grain bins stand hollow, their corrugated skins  
pocked with bullet-holes of rust, each dimple  
holding a single beetle, iridescent, dead.  

I kneel where the alfalfa should be knee-high—  
just stubble, yes, but not golden: gray-green,  
stiff as wire brushes left in rain.  
A jackrabbit freezes mid-leap, then bolts—  
not away, but *around* the same dry pivot  
where the center-pivot arm used to hum,  
now bent at the elbow, its nozzle plugged  
with a wad of tumbleweed, black and knotted  
like a fist full of drowned hair.  

My father’s boots hang on the barn door—  
not for luck, but because the soles dissolved  
in last year’s alkaline puddle, left only  
the uppers, stiff as taxidermied snakeskins,  
laced with twine made from unravelled baling twine.  

At dusk, the wind doesn’t sigh. It *scrapes*:  
a metal file drawn slow across concrete.  
It lifts the topsoil—not in clouds, but in sheets,  
thin as onion skin, translucent enough  
to see the fossilized root-tip of a cottonwood,  
fossilized *upside-down*, pointing skyward  
like a buried finger accusing the empty blue.  

No rain. No prayer. Just the fridge humming  
too loud in the kitchen, its compressor kicking  
on every ninety seconds—cold air leaking  
into the heat, a tiny, stubborn leak,  
like the one in the main line we never fixed,  
the one that hissed for three seasons  
before going silent, leaving only this:  
the weight of the hose reel, empty,  
and the faint, sweet-sour tang of plastic  
baking inside its hollow drum.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The Humming Vigil  

When sleep’s soft veil refuses to descend,  
And midnight bleeds to gray on hollow walls,  
I lie awake where quiet hours extend—  
No lullaby, no rest, no mercy calls.  
Then from the kitchen, low and unrelenting,  
A steady thrum begins—a muted drone—  
The fridge’s pulse, a ghostly, humming greeting,  
That turns the dark to metal, cold, and stone.  
It does not plead, nor pause, nor ask my leave;  
It simply *is*, as ancient as the stars—  
A monotone that neither lies nor weaves,  
Yet holds me fast beneath its silver bars.  
So I attend this vigil, stark and deep:  
The world sleeps on—I wake with hum and keep.

title: poem in tercets|a mother's hands
text:
Her hands, a map of years, crisscrossed with lines,
Where once they held me, soft as summer peaches,
Now bear the marks of time's relentless grind.

In kitchen light, her fingers dance on dough,
Kneading life into each ball and roll, the scent
Of yeast and warmth, a childhood I still know.

She sorts through photos, yellowed at the edges,
Tracing faces with a touch so light, it seems
To whisper secrets only she can pledge.

When illness came, those hands grew frail, yet strong—
A paradox of tenderness and steel,
Holding mine, a silent, steadfast song.

I see her garden, earth beneath her nails,
Tomatoes ripe, and roses in full bloom,
Each petal tended, every weed that wails.

And in the night, when shadows stretch and loom,
Her hands, a comfort, stroke my hair, a balm,
A lullaby, a shelter from the gloom.

title: prose poem|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Beekeeper in Winter  

He stands at the edge of the apiary, breath pluming like a small, lost hive. The hives are mounds of snow-draped silence—white shrouds over black wood, each lid weighted with frost, each entrance sealed by ice-glazed propolis. Inside, the bees are not sleeping; they are *holding*. A slow, dense cluster around the queen, trembling—not with cold, but with the ancient calculus of heat: wing-muscles flexing, shivering into warmth, passing it hand-to-hand, mouth-to-mouth, thorax-to-thorax, a living furnace banked low beneath the winter’s iron sky.  

His gloves are stiff with beeswax and cold. He presses a palm to the northern wall of Hive Three—not to open, never to disturb—but to feel the hum. Not sound, not vibration, but *presence*: a subsonic thrumming in the bone, the quiet pulse of life refusing erasure. Frost feathers his eyebrows. His beard holds tiny crystals, each one a captured breath, a suspended note.  

He remembers summer: the gold-dust air, the furious geometry of flight, the sting that bloomed hot and sudden on his wrist—a sacrament of attention. Now, the only gold is the honey he decanted last October, thick and amber in glass jars on the cellar shelf, glowing like captured sunset. It will feed them through February. It will feed *him*, too—when he stirs a spoonful into weak tea, the sweetness so deep it aches, a reminder that sweetness is not the absence of cold, but its tender, tenacious counterweight.  

At dusk, he walks back past the frozen creek, where the water moves unseen beneath the ice—dark, insistent, singing its low song to the roots. He does not pray. He watches. He waits. And in the stillness between one breath and the next, he hears it: not the buzz of wings, but the almost-sound of survival—soft as down, steady as gravity—keeping time with the earth’s slow turn toward light.

title: ghazal|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Desert Stars

The dunes exhale their ancient, silver sigh—  
each star a needle stitching night’s deep sky.  

No roof but void, no wall but wind’s low chant—  
the stars descend where thirsty camels lie.  

They do not blink—they burn with patient fire,  
cold lamps hung where lost caravans pass by.  

I named them once; they answered not my voice—  
just spun their light on dust and time and dry.  

My heart, a well with no reflection left,  
still holds the stars it cannot quench or buy.  

O constellations—do you know my name?  
Or am I just the dark you pierce and fly?

title: ode|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
In the quiet hum of fluorescent lights,
where shadows stretch like tired limbs,
she steps from the ward, her sneakers
whispering secrets to the linoleum.

Her scrubs, a canvas of accidental art—
ink smudges bloom like midnight violets,
a coffee stain maps an uncharted continent,
and the creases hold stories only she can read.

At the locker, her hands move with the grace
of a locksmith, each turn a ritual, a release.
The metal door swings open, a portal
to another world where the air is thick
with the scent of lavender and pine.

She peels off layers, each one a skin
shed in the heat of battle, until she stands
in the soft armor of street clothes,
a warrior disguised as a civilian.

Outside, the night wraps its cool arms
around her, and the stars blink like IV monitors,
steady, watchful. She walks through the parking lot,
her footsteps a syncopated rhythm,
a heartbeat that echoes through the city.

In her car, the dashboard glows softly,
a lighthouse in the dark, guiding her home.
The engine purrs, a cat curling at her feet,
and she drives, the road unwinding
like a long, deep breath, a sigh of relief.

title: villanelle|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Garden After the Gardener’s Death

The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine,  
The path is lost beneath the tangled green,  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

The gate hangs crooked, rusted on its line,  
While daisies crowd the stone where once was seen  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine.  

The fountain sleeps, its basin choked with silt and brine,  
No water sings—the dry stone holds no sheen—  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

The hollyhocks stand tall, then lean, decline,  
Their purple heads bow low where shadows lean;  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine.  

A sparrow nests inside the gardener’s hat, left behind,  
Its straw now frayed, its shape half-soft, half-thin—  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

Though time unspools what love so tightly bound,  
The soil remembers every seed it’s been:  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine,  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.

title: ballad in quatrains|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The porch swing’s rusted chain still groans  
like it did when I’d kick off my shoes,  
but the floorboard by the door—third from left—  
still squeaks the same damn tune, not news.  

Mom’s chipped mug’s gone from the cupboard shelf,  
but the stain’s still there, brown and thin,  
where she spilled chamomile every Tuesday  
while pretending the rent wasn’t due in.  

I packed the box marked “Dad’s Things”  
with one shirt, a bent spoon, his watch—  
stopped at 3:17, the day he walked out,  
not the day he came back, not quite.  

The lilacs by the fence are scraggly now,  
pruned wrong, half-drowned in clay,  
but their smell hit me sharp this morning—  
wet dirt, bruised petals, yesterday.  

The key’s cold in my palm, too small,  
fits the lock but won’t turn twice.  
I left it in the bowl by the stove,  
next to the loose button, the dried-up ice.

title: short lyric poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
In the city's quiet hum, a bus rolls by,
At two a.m., beneath the moonlit sky.
Its windows glow, like lanterns in the night,
Each pane a story, softly burning bright.

The driver's gaze, a steady, silent stream,
Guides through the shadows, as if in a dream.
Passengers few, each wrapped in thoughts so deep,
Their breaths like whispers, secrets they might keep.

Streets stretch ahead, in silver and in blue,
A canvas vast, with every hue anew.
The wheels, they sing a lullaby so low,
To all the souls who've found a place to go.

And as it fades, into the distant light,
A gentle peace descends, as soft as night.
For in its wake, this city bus bestows
A moment's calm, where only quiet flows.

title: short lyric poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Light  
The bleachers exhale dust and sweat,  
a thousand voices hum low—  
not quite song, not quite prayer—  
as the sun dips behind the pines.  
A whistle cuts the amber air.  
Someone’s mother adjusts her son’s collar,  
her fingers trembling just once.  

Third Quarter  
Grass stains bloom on white jerseys,  
helmets gleam like wet river stones.  
The quarterback stumbles, rises,  
spits grass and grins.  
A boy in the front row clutches his father’s cap,  
too small for the roar, too big to look away.  
The scoreboard flickers: 14–10.  
Time bends, thick as honey.  

After the Whistle  
Lights blaze cold now, emptying fast—  
paper cups swirl in the wind,  
a lone glove lies abandoned near the goalpost.  
Two teams shake hands, helmets under arms,  
faces streaked with mud and something softer.  
Somewhere, a radio plays static and a distant game.  
We walk home slow,  
carrying the echo like a shared secret.

title: villanelle|grief after a dog dies
text:
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge,  
a coiled question mark no one answers now.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

I found your favorite sock beneath the fridge—  
still warm where fur once snagged the rubber sole.  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  

At dusk, the neighbor’s terrier barks, and I flinch  
like a nerve exposed, raw in the thinning air.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

The vet’s receipt curls at the edge of the counter:  
*Euthanasia, sedation, cremation fee.*  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  

I vacuumed twice today—just to hear the hum,  
the only sound that doesn’t name your name.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

Last night, I dreamed you were a cracked sidewalk,  
warm asphalt yielding under my bare feet.  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.

title: spoken-word poem|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
A Library on a Sunday Afternoon

In the hush of pages turned, in whispers soft and light,
Where time itself seems to pause, to bask in gentle quiet,
Sits the library, a sanctuary of thoughts unspoken,
A harbor for dreams, under the watch of book spines broken.

Here, where the sun's fingers stretch, lazy and long,
Casting shadows that dance upon stories strong,
Patrons wander, like silent specters of old,
Seeking solace in tales, bold and cold.

The air is thick with the scent of ink and paper,
A fragrance that clings, an eternal caper.
Each breath taken, a sip from the well of knowledge,
Nourishing minds, in this haven of silence and college.

Children, eyes wide with wonder, explore realms afar,
Their imaginations sparked by each word, like a star.
Elders, too, find comfort in familiar lines,
Reliving memories, through verses that shine.

Outside, the world rushes, in chaos and noise,
But within these walls, there's only the choice
To lose oneself in the magic, the mystery, the might,
Of words penned down, in black and white.

As afternoon fades into evening's embrace,
This temple of wisdom remains in its place,
A beacon for those who seek understanding and peace,
In the heart of the city, where all worries cease.

title: sequence of haiku|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First snow—  
the cracked asphalt gleams  
under sodium light.  

My coffee cup’s lid  
still says “St. Vincent’s”  
faded blue, chipped rim.  

That kid in 3B  
left footprints dragging  
toward the bus stop.  

Wind lifts a single glove  
from the overflow lot—  
blue, small, missing fingers.  

Snow on the ER awning  
melts slow, then drips  
onto the “No Loitering” sign.

title: sequence of haiku|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Subway Sequence  

Steel throat exhales steam—  
a thousand breaths condense, then fade—  
my coat brushes yours.  

Neon bleeds through glass—  
a woman’s earbuds pulse low;  
her knuckles whiten.  

Rain-streaked tunnel dark—  
the train sways, a tired spine—  
we hold the same pole.  

A child points: *Look! Light!*  
and for three stops, we are air—  
then doors sigh open.

title: dramatic monologue|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Rust Psalm

The whistle’s gone. Not broken—*gone*.  
No iron lung to heave the dawn,  
no steam-hiss hymn to stitch the gray,  
no clang of gears that marked the day.  
Just silence—thick as factory dust,  
settled deep in every crust  
of brick and bone and boarded glass,  
where time itself has ground to pass.

I walk the street where men once marched  
in grease-stained boots, shoulders arched—  
not proud, but *known*: the lathe-man, welder,  
foreman’s nod, the shift’s slow elder.  
Now windows gape like hollow eyes,  
their panes all starred with shattered skies.  
The smokestack stands—a blackened spine,  
a monument to what was *mine*,  
to what was *ours*, to what we built  
with calloused hands and sleepless guilt  
for wages thin and futures thin,  
while hope ran low and bosses grinned.

The diner’s open—barely—light  
a single bulb, too weak, too white.  
Marla pours coffee, cold and thin,  
and doesn’t ask who’s left within.  
She knows. We all do. Names erased  
from payrolls, then from memory’s space:  
Joe’s truck’s been sold, his daughter fled  
to Atlanta, beds unmade, unread  
college brochures on the floor.  
Maggie’s still here—she cleans the store  
that sells no goods but ghosts and glue,  
and hums a tune she can’t get through.

Some nights I stand beneath that stack,  
press palm to rust—still warm, not slack—  
as if the furnace breathes below,  
a phantom heat no one will know.  
But it’s just wind through broken vents,  
the town’s last sigh, its slow descent  
into the hush where engines slept,  
where promises were over-kept,  
where children learn the alphabet  
from faded signs: *“Quality. Integrity. Growth.”*  
All rusted out. All stripped. All lost.  

We don’t rage. Not anymore.  
We just hold the quiet door—  
and wait for something new to rise,  
or for the silence to grow wise.

title: blank verse meditation|grief after a dog dies
text:
After the Last Walk  

The leash still hangs beside the back door—  
a coil of worn nylon, stiff with dried mud,  
its brass clasp dulled, its buckle cold to touch.  
I reach for it each morning, then pause,  
my hand suspended in the quiet air,  
as if the weight of habit might still summon  
the soft thud of paws on linoleum,  
the eager whine before the latch clicks up.  

The house is too large now, too still.  
No warm weight pressed against my knee at dusk,  
no nose nudging my wrist for a scratch behind the ear—  
just silence, thick and unrelenting,  
filling corners where her shadow used to pool.  

I find her hair caught in the bristles of the brush,  
a tangle of gold and gray, fine as spun light.  
I hold it—not to keep, but to remember  
how it caught the sun when she ran,  
how it softened under my palm when she slept,  
how it drifted, weightless, from her coat  
in the weeks before the vet’s hushed voice,  
before the final, gentle letting go.  

Grief is not a storm—it is the slow seep of tide  
into dry sand: quiet, inevitable,  
leaving hollows no filling can restore.  
I do not weep for what is gone,  
but for the ordinary miracles I mistook for given:  
the way she waited, always,  
not for treats or praise, but for *me*—  
for my breath, my step, my return.  
She loved without condition,  
lived without pretense,  
died without ceremony—  
and in that simple, faithful brevity,  
taught me how deeply love can root  
in the small, unremarkable earth of daily things.  

So I walk alone now,  
but carry her pace inside me—  
a rhythm beneath my ribs,  
a warmth where her head once rested,  
a quiet certainty:  
some bonds do not end with breath,  
but deepen, unseen,  
like roots in dark soil,  
holding the ground together  
long after the green has faded.

title: spoken-word poem|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
In the shadow of smokestacks, now cold and gray,
Echoes of hammers, silence fills the day.
Rusty gates hang open, like mouths agape,
Whispering secrets of a time that escaped.

Old man Jenkins, he used to walk with pride,
Wore his coveralls like a badge, chest wide.
Now he shuffles, eyes down, hands in pockets deep,
Searching for coins, or maybe just sleep.

The diner’s empty, save for Betty's frown,
Coffee grows stale, her dreams are brown.
She talks to ghosts, sips from cracked mugs,
Remembers laughter, but can't find the hugs.

Kids on the street, no future in sight,
Chalk drawings on pavement, their only light.
Factory playground, twisted metal and rust,
A jungle gym for the lost, the forgotten, the just.

Even the river, once blue, now gray,
Carries the town’s sorrows, day by day.
Fish float belly up, and the ducks have flown,
Leaving behind a mirror, showing what we’ve grown.

At night, the stars still shine, indifferent, cold,
As if they’ve seen this story, a hundred times told.
But in the dark, there’s a flicker, a spark,
Maybe it’s hope, or maybe just heart.

title: sequence of haiku|watching a parent grow old
text:
Sequence of Haiku: Watching You Grow Old  

First light—  
your hand trembles holding the teacup,  
steam rising like breath.  

Winter window—  
frost etches fragile branches  
on the glass you wipe.  

Your glasses fog—  
you peer at my face, then smile,  
mistaking my name.  

Folded sweater—  
sleeves too long, wool soft as down,  
still smelling of lavender.  

Empty chair—  
the newspaper lies open,  
page turned by wind.

title: dramatic monologue|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
I. The Last Stop Before Dawn  
The engine hums a low, tired hymn,  
headlights slicing fog like dull knives—  
no one boards but the rain,  
and the ghost of a man who checks his watch  
then vanishes into the wet brick wall.  
I steer the empty aisle,  
fingers white on the wheel’s cold rim,  
while the fare box clicks open and shut,  
open and shut,  
though no coin has dropped in hours.

II. The One Who Rides the Line  
She sits behind me, third row left,  
coat too thin for this hour,  
staring at her reflection in the black window—  
not seeing herself, but something moving just beyond the glass:  
a flicker, a shadow with no source.  
She whispers to the seat beside her,  
names I don’t recognize,  
and when she stands to exit,  
her breath fogs the glass in the shape of a door.  
I don’t look back.  
I never do.

III. Terminal Silence  
The depot lights buzz like trapped wasps.  
I kill the engine.  
The bus sighs—air brakes exhale,  
doors wheeze shut,  
and for three breaths, it is still:  
no radio static, no distant siren,  
just the slow drip of condensation  
from the roof vent onto the floor mat.  
Then the radio crackles—  
*“Driver, you’re clear for layover.”*  
I don’t answer.  
I rest my forehead on the wheel  
and count the seconds until the next shift begins,  
until the city remembers it needs us again.

title: dramatic monologue|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean's Fury

Beneath the shroud of night, I rise and swell,
A titan clad in tempests, waves my crest.
I roar with voices old as time itself,
And in my heart, a storm that knows no rest.

The heavens weep their tears into my depths,
As lightning scythes the sky with fiery hands.
My breath is wind, a howling, bitter song,
That shatters ships and scatters ocean sands.

Oh, hear me, land-dwellers, in your safety,
For I am chaos, I am fear, I am might.
No anchor holds, no lighthouse pierces through,
When I, the sea, decide to claim the night.

The gulls have fled, the dolphins seek the deep,
But I, undaunted, rage against the shore.
My fury builds, a crescendo of despair,
Till every soul on earth shall know my roar.

Yet in my wrath, there lies a mournful plea,
To be understood, to not be feared, but known.
For even oceans long for peace at times,
In storms, we find our strength, and then are grown.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|time and memory
text:
Sonnet for the Clock That Swallowed My Keys  

The second hand gnaws rust from iron hinges—  
not metaphor, but actual flakes that fall  
like dandruff off a rusted bicycle chain  
I left last spring behind the garage wall.  

My mother’s voice arrives via landline static:  
a dial tone hums beneath her “How are you?”  
as if the wire itself remembers  
the exact pitch of her laugh, worn thin and true.  

That photo—faded at the corners, bent—  
shows me knee-deep in creek-muck, grinning,  
holding a crayfish whose claws still pinch  
the air between thumb and forefinger,  
though the creature’s long dissolved to silt.  

Time isn’t sand. It’s the fridge light’s buzz  
that stays on after the door’s shut—  
a small, persistent voltage in the dark,  
humming the shape of what was,  
but not quite *what*.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The light slants low—three o’clock, maybe four—  
and hits the dust motes dancing over Dewey.  
I’m in 821.3 again, though I swore  
I’d skip the Victorians today. My knee  
aches where the old splinter dug in, back  
in ’09, prying loose that warped floorboard  
behind the microfiche reader (still black  
and humming faintly, like a tired chord).  
Mrs. Gable’s knitting needles click-clack  
near the biography shelves—blue yarn, slow pace.  
A kid drops a volume of Auden; it cracks  
like dry twigs underfoot. No one looks up.  
The radiator hisses steam, then sighs.  
I trace the watermark on this page—half-erased,  
a ghostly lily, pressed by someone’s thumb  
who never signed their name, just left it there.

title: elegy|drought on a family farm
text:
Beneath the sun's relentless, scorching eye,
The fields lie barren, earth as cracked and dry
As ancient parchment, whispering of loss.
No verdant life, no green to comfort us.

The once proud stalks, now withered, pale, and thin,
Stand like the ghosts of seasons long since spun.
Their leaves, a brittle memory, cling on
To stems that bend beneath the weight of none.

The well, our lifeline, silent, deep, and still,
Reflects the sky, a mirror to despair.
Its waters, once so plentiful, now shrill,
A mocking echo of what used to be there.

Our hands, calloused, worn from endless toil,
Reach out in vain to skies too blue, too vast.
Each cloud that forms, then fades, without recoil,
Leaves in its wake a sorrow that will last.

The old barn stands, a sentinel of time,
Its weathered boards a testament to years
Of laughter, tears, and stories left behind,
Now shadows dance where once was joyous cheer.

At dusk, the horizon paints a mournful scene,
A palette of reds and oranges, fierce, yet cold.
It speaks of endings, of what might have been,
A canvas splashed with dreams that never hold.

And in the night, when stars pierce through the dark,
We gather 'round, our hearts both heavy, light.
In whispered tones, we share the day's stark mark,
And find in silence, strength to face the night.

title: poem in tercets|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
I. Arrival  
The sky unspools its gray and thin,  
a hush descends—not silence, but the weight  
of waiting held between breaths and skin.  

II. Landing  
Flakes alight on windshields, cold and slight,  
on gurney wheels, on cigarette ash,  
on the cracked asphalt where light  
refuses to stay—too frail, too brief, too rash.  

III. After  
A child’s glove lies half-buried, blue and small,  
a nurse pauses, breath pluming, then walks on—  
the lot now soft, white, holding nothing at all.

title: blank verse meditation|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
Midnight Transit

The engine hums—a low and steady thrum—  
a pulse beneath the floorboards, worn and thin.  
No driver speaks; his gaze stays fixed ahead,  
where sodium lights smear yellow on the wet street.  
A woman nods against the fogged-up glass,  
her coat pulled tight, a grocery bag slack  
beside her boots. Her breath fogs, fades, returns.  

Two youths sit close but do not touch—  
one scrolls a screen’s cold glow across his face,  
the other stares past rows of empty seats,  
past ads for things no one buys at this hour:  
vacations, loans, bright teeth, quick fixes—all  
unreal as mist that gathers on the windows.  

The bus lurches, brakes sigh, a pause too long—  
then rolls again through blocks of shuttered shops,  
past fire escapes like ribs against brick walls,  
past alleys where the wind stirs crumpled paper,  
past stoops where silence settles, thick and deep,  
as if the city holds its breath between dreams.  

No sirens now. No shouts. Just rain’s soft tap  
on roof and glass, the rhythm of the wipers,  
left-right, left-right—the only conversation.  
We move through sleep like ghosts inside a shell,  
carried forward—not toward home, not yet,  
but through the hush where time itself slows down,  
and every soul aboard becomes a thought  
the city thinks, then lets go, softly, on.

title: sequence of haiku|the sound of a train at night
text:
Steel whispers through dark,  
City's heartbeat fades, distant—  
Tracks hum lullabies.

Night air stirs, alive,  
Vibrations cradle the moonlight—  
Whispers of departure.

Rumbling bass notes dance,  
Neon signs flicker in sync—  
Silent buildings sway.

title: prose poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
First Gear  

The car is a nervous animal, engine humming low in the driveway’s quiet. He adjusts the seat—not too far, not too close—his hand steady on the wheel as if holding a bird that might startle. She grips the rim, knuckles pale, breath shallow. “Eyes up,” he says, not unkindly, and she lifts her gaze from the hood to the empty street ahead, where dandelions push through cracked asphalt like tiny, stubborn stars. He guides her hands: ten and two, not nine and three, because he remembers his own father saying, *This is how you hold something precious without squeezing it dry*. The clutch bites, the engine stutters, the car lurches forward—then stalls. She flinches. He doesn’t sigh. He turns the key again, soft and sure. “Again,” he says, and means *again*, not *try harder*, not *don’t fail*. Her foot finds the pedal’s resistance, her shoulders drop an inch, her left hand releases just enough to let the wheel breathe. They roll past the oak where he once scraped his first fender, past the mailbox painted with chipped blue letters, past the neighbor’s dog who barks but doesn’t chase. No destination. Just this: the hum, the light on the dash, the way her reflection in the windshield holds his eyes for a second—steady, startled, already learning how to carry the weight of motion, how to steer not just metal and glass, but the quiet, trembling space between instruction and trust.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the night shift at a diner
text:
The Midnight Griddle’s Lament

When midnight’s veil doth cloak the weary street,  
And all the world doth slumber, deep and still,  
There stands a diner—humble, worn, and sweet—  
Where coffee steams and neon hums its will.  
The fryer hisses like a dragon caged,  
The grill spits sparks in blue and amber light;  
A waitress, tired but never disengaged,  
Moves through the hush with purpose, calm, and might.  
Two truckers lean on stools, their faces lined  
With miles and silence, sipping pie and tea;  
A student scribbles, sleepless, half-entwined  
With textbooks, lost in thought’s austerity.  
O night-shift souls! Though stars withdraw from sight,  
You keep the flame alight—both warm and bright.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|hope after a long illness
text:
In the shadow of the old oak, where whispers cling to bark,
A spider weaves her fragile lace, each strand a silver arc.
Beneath the earth, roots stretch and groan, a hidden, silent choir,
And in this quiet, I find my breath, a firefly’s soft light.

The air is thick with jasmine scent, a ghost of summers past,
Yet here, amidst the winter’s chill, a single bloom holds fast.
It speaks in colors, not in words, a language deep and true,
A promise that the world will turn, and spring will come anew.

My body, once a heavy stone, now feels the feather’s touch,
A gentle breeze that stirs the leaves, a slow and steady crutch.
The moon, a pearl in the night sky, casts shadows on the ground,
A map of paths I’ve yet to walk, of wounds that heal unbound.

In the distance, a train’s low hum, a pulse beneath the skin,
Carrying strangers through the dark, their dreams and hopes within.
I hear their laughter, faint and far, a melody that floats,
A symphony of human hearts, a chorus of our notes.

Here, in the stillness, I am found, a traveler in repose,
With every step, a new horizon, a journey that unfolds.
Hope, a wildflower in the field, blooms where the soil is rich,
A testament to life’s tenacity, a gift I hold and stitch.

title: villanelle|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
A Lost Glove on a Fence Post

A lost glove hangs on a fence post, thin and worn,  
Its fingers curled as if grasping the air—  
A ghost of warmth where no hand is borne.  

The wind combs through its frayed and faded horn,  
While sparrows pause, then flicker, light and fair;  
A lost glove hangs on a fence post, thin and worn.  

No owner comes at dusk or break of morn,  
No call, no search, no whispered, “Where’s it there?”—  
A ghost of warmth where no hand is borne.  

It holds the shape of absence, sharp and torn,  
A hollow map of touch beyond compare;  
A lost glove hangs on a fence post, thin and worn.  

Rain darkens wool, sun bleaches threadbare, worn—  
Yet still it clings, though all else drifts elsewhere;  
A ghost of warmth where no hand is borne.  

So time lets go what time cannot adorn:  
One glove remains—unclaimed, unloosed, unaware.  
A lost glove hangs on a fence post, thin and worn,  
A ghost of warmth where no hand is borne.

title: short untitled lowercase poem in the style of modern Instagram poetry books|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
my scrubs smell like antiseptic  
and the burnt sugar of the coffee  
i forgot to drink before the code  
in 4b  

my left knee aches where the gurney wheel  
jammed into it during the transfer  
from bed to stretcher—  
no one saw.  

i counted three breaths for mrs. lynch  
while she held my wrist like a lifeline  
then handed her son the discharge papers  
with a pen that leaked blue ink  
all over his thumb  

the break room fridge hums  
a low C that vibrates in my molars  
i eat cold lasagna from the container  
with the dented lid  
and lick tomato sauce off my knuckle  
because the sink’s out again  

my badge is warm from my pocket  
my hair smells like hand sanitizer  
and something faintly floral—  
probably the lilac soap in the med cart  
that no one ever uses except me  

i walk past the empty chairs  
in the waiting room  
where the clock says 7:03  
but my body says 3:17  
and my phone says  
*you have 2 unread texts*  
both from my sister  
both unopened

title: dramatic monologue|time and memory
text:
I. The Clockmaker’s Confession  
My hands have wound a thousand gears,  
yet never caught the second slipping—  
that silver fish through fingers’ net.  
I polish brass, I calibrate the fall  
of weighted chains, I name each tick a truth—  
but when the hour strikes, it’s always yesterday  
knocking at the door I thought I locked.  

II. The Photograph Album  
This page holds summer: you, barefoot, grinning,  
sand in your hair, ice melting down your wrist.  
I press my thumb where your smile begins—  
the paper warms, then cools.  
The date on the back is wrong.  
I remember the light wrong.  
I remember you taller.  
The album doesn’t lie;  
it simply forgets to breathe.  

III. The Last Watch  
It stopped at 3:17—the exact minute  
you turned to wave, then walked beyond the gate.  
I keep it wound. I hold it to my ear.  
Silence, of course.  
But sometimes—just before sleep—  
a phantom chime, a tremor in the glass,  
and for one breath, the hands rush backward,  
not to fix the time,  
but to unmake the leaving.

title: ballad in quatrains|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
The sodium lights hum low and thin,  
a sickly yellow bruise on black—  
then white begins: not flake, but spin,  
a million tiny plastic sacks.  

They catch on wheel-well rust, on cracks  
where oil-slick rainbows coil and weep,  
on cigarette butts stamped to ash,  
on cracked vinyl where toddlers sleep.  

A gurney’s left outside—its wheels  
still spinning slow, a ghostly whine—  
while snow fills the hollows of its steel,  
like sugar poured in a coffee line.  

My breath fogs the glass, then clears—  
just long enough to see a nurse  
pull hood up, step past the ER doors,  
her scrubs stained with iodine and verse.  

No hush falls. Sirens stitch the air.  
A bagged IV pole leans, half-buried,  
its drip chamber frozen mid-fall—  
a clear, hard tear no one has carried.

title: short lyric poem|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Echoes of Industry

In streets where once machines hummed loud,
Silence now wears the fading shroud.
Windows, like eyes, all blank and still,
Gaze at the world with a vacant chill.

Rusted gates no longer swing wide,
Secrets held by the river's side.
Workers' dreams, now scattered dust,
In the air, a whisper, a rustle, a hush.

Smokestack shadows stretch so long,
Over homes where laughter's gone.
Yet, in the quiet, hope does creep,
A seed beneath the concrete deep.

title: dramatic monologue|watching a parent grow old
text:
The teacup trembles—not the cup, the *hand* holding it.  
That blue-and-white one with the chip on the rim, the one Mom dropped in ’98 when the furnace blew and the house went black and she laughed, saying, “Well, that’s one less thing to dust.”  

Now her knuckles are swollen knots, like old roots pushing up through sidewalk cracks.  
She tries to lift the kettle—stainless steel, dented near the spout from when Dad knocked it off the stove with his elbow—and her wrist bends sideways, just a little, like a hinge gone soft.  
I watch. I don’t reach. Not yet.  

Her hair’s gone that brittle silver-grey, but not evenly—there’s still a stubborn patch of brown behind her left ear, like a secret she forgot to tell me about.  
And her slippers: mismatched. Left foot, faded purple flannel with one embroidered daisy half-unraveled. Right foot, navy wool, slightly too big, dragging a little on the linoleum. She doesn’t notice. Or maybe she does, and it’s easier to let it drag.  

Yesterday she asked me, voice thin as rice paper, “Did you water the geraniums?”  
I said yes.  
She nodded, then stared at the window for three full minutes while the rain streaked the glass like tears someone else had cried.  
The geraniums are dead. Wilted, brown at the stems. I haven’t touched them since August.  

She hums sometimes—off-key, a fragment of “Danny Boy,” or the theme from *The Brady Bunch*, or once, last Tuesday, the jingle for that detergent with the orange box. No reason. Just air moving through dry pipes.  

I found her standing in the garage last week, holding Dad’s old tape measure open to 5’10”, staring at the mark like it was a name she’d forgotten how to spell.  
She didn’t say his name. Didn’t cry. Just closed the tape with a soft *shhk* and put it back in the drawer where the screwdrivers live, right next to the rusted Phillips head she uses to tighten the loose hinge on the pantry door—even though the hinge isn’t loose. It hasn’t been, in years.  

Sometimes, when she sleeps, her mouth hangs open just a fraction.  
A tiny, wet gap.  
I see the denture ridge—the pink line where the gum ends—and the way her lower lip trembles, even now, even in sleep, like something’s still trying to speak, but the words got lost somewhere between the throat and the tongue.  

I pour her tea.  
She takes it.  
Her thumb brushes mine—dry, warm, papery—and I feel the exact weight of every year stacked behind that touch.  
Not heavy. Not light.  
Just there.  
Like the dust motes in the afternoon sun, hanging, not falling, not rising—just *there*, turning slow in the light, until the light shifts, and they’re gone.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
Last Light  

You polish the lens one final time—  
not for duty, but for love:  
the brass cold under your palms,  
the prisms catching the dusk like trapped breath.  

Outside, the sea exhales—  
a slow, salt-thick sigh against black rocks.  
The lamp is lit. Not by switch, but ritual:  
wick trimmed, oil poured, flame coaxed  
into a steady, sovereign gold.  

You stand where generations stood—  
boots worn thin at the heel,  
logbook open to a blank page,  
pen resting beside the date: *Tonight.*  

No storm gathers. Just wind,  
just the old tower humming low in its bones,  
just the light—  
unblinking, unburdened—  
casting its long, lean arm across the water,  
not to warn, but to witness:  
this shore, this sky, this quiet surrender.  

When you turn the key in the door,  
you do not look back.  
The beam keeps turning.  
It does not need you to hold it.  
It only asks that you be held—  
once, wholly—  
by the dark you leave behind,  
and the light you set free.

title: meditative lyric that reads like a translation of a German poem|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. The Morning's Embrace

In the quiet dawn, where whispers blend,
Rises a scent, warm and without end.
Cinnamon swirls with dough so light,
A gentle hug from morning’s first light.

 II. Afternoon Whispers

Noon sun spills through the windowpane,
Herbs dance in pots, a fragrant rain.
Thyme and rosemary, sage and dill,
Stories told by each leaf, until
The kitchen fills with tales untold,
Of hands that stir, of hearts grown old.

 III. Evening Lullaby

As twilight weaves its tender spell,
The air with sweet aromas swells.
Apple pie, a golden dream,
Whispers softly, like a stream.
In every crumb, in every bite,
Lies a memory, soft and bright.

title: prose poem|the sound of a train at night
text:
Midnight Iron Song

It begins as a tremor in the earth—less heard than felt, a slow pulse rising through the soles of bare feet on cold porch wood. Then, a low hum, like the world clearing its throat. Distant, but insistent: a metallic sigh drawn long across the dark. The rails breathe steam into the chill air; the ties exhale damp cedar and rust.

Closer now—the clatter sharpens, a staccato rattle of couplings, the groan of brakes easing into their own weight. Headlights pierce the black not as light but as *presence*: two white wounds in the night’s fabric, widening, blinding, then sliding past like eyes that do not see you—only the curve ahead, the switch, the station name fading into silence before it’s spoken.

The whistle comes last—not a call, but a release: a long, lonesome vowel stretched thin over fields where corn stalks shiver and owls hold their breath. It doesn’t fade so much as unravel—first the high edge fraying, then the body thinning to breath, then nothing but the after-ring in the ears, the hollow echo in the ribs.

And then: only the settling. Gravel shifting. A single spark hissing in the dark. The wind remembering the shape of speed. You stand there, still humming—not with sound, but with absence—while the night stitches itself back together, thread by slow, silver thread.

title: villanelle|grief after a dog dies
text:
In the room where your leash hangs, silence weighs,
Your paw prints still in mud by the back door.
I trace them, each a ghost of happier days.

The park's too quiet now; no barks, no play,
Just empty paths that echo with my grief.
In the room where your leash hangs, silence weighs.

Your collar lies untouched, its tags displayed
Like relics of a time that can't return.
Your paw prints still in mud by the back door.

At night, I swear I hear your nails on stairs,
A phantom rustle, tail thumping in dreams.
In the room where your leash hangs, silence weighs.

But morning brings the ache, the empty chair,
The walks we won't take, and the games we've ceased.
Your paw prints still in mud by the back door.

How do I fill this house, these hollow hours?
The world's grown colder, darker, without you.
In the room where your leash hangs, silence weighs,
Your paw prints still in mud by the back door.

title: spoken-word poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
“First Gear”  

The leather seat still holds the ghost of his palms—  
warm, calloused, resting low on the wheel like anchors.  
Outside, rain smears the world into watercolor:  
streetlights bleed gold into wet asphalt,  
a stop sign bleeds red,  
and the engine hums—not a roar, but a held breath.  

She’s seventeen, knuckles white on the steering wheel,  
hair pulled back too tight,  
breath catching where her collarbone dips—  
a shallow well of nerves.  
He doesn’t say *relax*.  
He says, *Feel the clutch bite.*  
His left hand hovers—not touching—just above her knee,  
a silent semaphore: *I am here, but I will not steer.*  

She presses the gas. The car lurches—  
a startled bird flapping sideways—  
and he exhales, slow, through his nose,  
like releasing smoke from a pipe long unlit.  
No correction. No sigh. Just:  
*That’s the engine telling you it’s ready.  
Listen. Not with your ears—with your spine.*  

Her foot trembles on the pedal.  
He watches her eyes—not the road, not the mirror—  
but the way her gaze flickers,  
how she blinks twice before turning her head,  
how her throat moves when she swallows down the word *sorry*  
before she’s even spoken it.  

At the empty intersection, she stops—  
too far back, too still—  
and he finally rests his hand, light as a moth’s wing,  
on the small of her back.  
Not guiding.  
Bearing witness.  

The wipers sweep left, right, left—  
a metronome for this new rhythm:  
her hands learning the language of torque and turn,  
his silence learning the grammar of release.  

Later, when she parks—smooth, steady, alone—  
he opens his door, steps out,  
lets the cold air rush in.  
Doesn’t hug her. Doesn’t praise.  
Just leans in, taps the dashboard twice—  
*thump-thump*, like a heartbeat finding its own time—  
and says,  
*You drove us home.*  

Not *we drove*.  
*You.*  

The keys are warm in her palm.  
The rearview holds his face, receding—  
not smaller, but softer—  
as if, for the first time,  
he is letting her see him  
without the rearview.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
I. V-Formation Over Ice  
You watch them cleave the brittle air—  
a black stitch pulling northward,  
wings beating time against the cold.  
The lake below is glass and ghost,  
still as held breath,  
yet beneath its surface, water remembers flow.  
*You, too, carry ancient routes in your bones.*  

II. The Hollow Between Wingtips  
One goose breaks formation—  
not lost, but looping low,  
circling the ice’s fractured edge  
where light catches the hairline cracks.  
You hold your own pause,  
your own necessary drift.  
*Healing is not straight flight, but the courage to turn—and trust the flock will wait.*  

III. Echo After Landing  
They vanish beyond the pines.  
Only silence remains—  
and the faintest tremor in the ice,  
as if the lake, too, exhaled.  
You stand warmer now,  
not because the wind softened,  
but because you remembered:  
*you are both the journey and the shore it returns to.*

title: dramatic monologue|the first heartbreak
text:
The Echoes of My First Goodbye

In the quiet corners of my memory, you linger,
A shadow cast by the setting sun of our youth.
Where once was light, now only darkness clings,
For in your absence, I found the depth of night.

Your laughter, a melody that danced through time,
Now plays as a dirge, slow and sorrowful.
Each note, a reminder of what once was mine,
Of stolen kisses under the willow.

How could love, so tender, turn to pain?
Like a rose, its beauty marred by thorns.
I reached for petals, but felt only the sting,
Left bleeding, as the garden of my heart mourns.

You were my first, in every sense, my all,
The author of a story without an end.
But now, the pages are blank, the ink has dried,
Our tale, a whisper on the wind, sent.

Yet, in this silence, there's a strange solace,
A bittersweet acceptance of the fall.
For even in heartbreak, there is grace,
And from these ashes, I will rise, stand tall.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
V-Formation Over Black Ice  

Their wings don’t cleave the air—they *scrape* it, thin  
and rasping, like a file on frozen steel.  
Below, the lake’s a slab of shattered gin,  
cracks webbing out where pressure made it reel.  
No honking—just the hollow *thwip-thwip-thwip*  
of feathers snapping taut against the gale,  
a sound like plastic bags caught in a grip  
of wind that smells of diesel, road-salt, rail.  

One bird dips low—not grace, but torque, a lurch—  
its shadow skims the ice: a ragged stain,  
a smear of charcoal on the glassy church  
of water turned to something cold and plain.  
They pass. The lake reseals. No ripple stays.  
Just cold light stitching up the broken days.

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|the first heartbreak
text:
I remember the exact shade of blue in the chipped enamel mug you left behind—  
not cobalt, not navy, but that bruised, watery blue  
like the sky right before a thunderstorm that never breaks,  
the kind that just hangs, thick and humming, over the parking lot behind the laundromat  
where I folded your flannel shirt three times, then unfolded it,  
then folded it again, wrong, the cuff inside-out,  
and didn’t throw it away.  

I remember the smell of burnt toast every Tuesday at 7:13 a.m.  
because that’s when the toaster in my apartment decided to grieve with me,  
spitting out blackened rectangles like little charcoal prayers,  
and I’d eat them anyway, dry, no butter, just the ash-taste,  
just to feel something that wasn’t the hollow behind my ribs  
when the phone stayed silent through three full rings, then voicemail,  
then the beep that sounded exactly like the one before it,  
and the one before that.  

I remember the way my left knee cracked—*pop-hiss*—  
every time I stood up from the floor of your old studio apartment,  
where we’d sat cross-legged on that thrift-store rug,  
its pattern half-eaten by moths,  
and you said *I don’t know how to want two things at once*,  
and I nodded, because I knew the grammar of that sentence,  
knew its syntax, its weight, its polite, devastating comma,  
but didn’t know yet that my body would start memorizing absence  
like muscle memory:  
the empty space beside me on the bus bench,  
the untouched half of the shared fries cooling in the paper boat,  
the way my hand still lifted—palm up, open—  
when the door clicked shut behind you for the last time,  
as if waiting for keys I’d already given back.  

I remember the song that played twice in one afternoon—  
“Dust in the Wind,” of all things—  
once on the busted speaker of the ’98 Corolla I borrowed from my cousin,  
once on the tinny earbud of my brother’s discarded iPod Nano,  
both times making me swerve slightly, not enough to hit anything,  
just enough to feel the road lurch under me,  
like gravity had loosened its grip for three minutes and twenty-seven seconds.  

I remember the grocery list I wrote on the back of your last birthday card:  
*eggs, oat milk, bandaids (small), that weird mint toothpaste you liked,  
lightbulbs (the warm kind, not the hospital kind),  
a new shower curtain (mine has a stain shaped like Lake Michigan),  
a reason to wear the red sweater again.*  

I remember the way my voice changed—not cracked, not deepened—  
but flattened, like someone had pressed it between two library books  
for too long,  
so that when I ordered coffee, I’d say *large, black, no lid*  
and the barista would pause, glance up, and say *you okay?*  
and I’d say *yeah, just tired*,  
which was true, but not the truth,  
and she’d nod like she knew the difference  
but wouldn’t name it.  

I remember the text I typed and deleted seventeen times:  
*Did you mean what you said about the silence being louder than words?*  
Then *Do you miss the way I hum off-key in the shower?*  
Then *Is it weird that I still know your Wi-Fi password?*  
Then *I walked past the record store and didn’t go in.*  
Then *I went in. Bought the Bowie album you hated.*  
Then *I played it. Turned it off at “Lady Grinning Soul.”*  
Then *I think I’m learning how to hold space for a person who isn’t there.*  
Then *I think I’m terrible at it.*  

I remember the first time I saw you after—  
not planned, not accidental, just *there*,  
leaning against the brick wall outside the post office,  
talking to someone else, laughing, head tilted,  
and how my feet locked, not from shock, not from pain,  
but from pure, dumb biology—  
like my nervous system had forgotten how to signal *move*  
and just kept whispering *look, look, look*,  
even though my eyes already knew the shape of your collarbone,  
the way your left earlobe stuck out just a fraction more,  
the exact number of freckles scattered across your nose in July light.  

I remember the silence after the silence—  
not peaceful, not clean—  
but thick, like walking through wet wool,  
full of static and half-heard frequencies:  
the refrigerator humming its low C-sharp,  
the neighbor’s dog barking at nothing at 3:44 a.m.,  
the sound of my own breath catching, not sobbing, not sighing,  
just… snagging, like thread on a rough seam.  

I remember the dream where we were back in your kitchen,  
making grilled cheese, and the bread burned,  
and instead of cursing, you laughed,  
and wiped the smoke alarm with a dish towel,  
and said *let’s eat it anyway*,  
and I woke up with the taste of charred cheddar on my tongue,  
and the certainty—not hope, not longing—  
that some part of me would always be standing there,  
holding the spatula,  
waiting for the butter to bubble,  
waiting for the sizzle,  
waiting for the smoke,  
waiting for you to say *let’s eat it anyway*,  
even though you weren’t there,  
even though the stove was cold,  
even though the spatula was just wood and heat and memory,  
and nothing else.

title: dramatic monologue|a beekeeper in winter
text:
In the hush of winter, when the world is sheathed in white,
And silence swallows sound like a ravenous night,
I stand amidst my apiaries, a keeper of the still,
Where once a buzz of life danced to summer's will.

The hives, now empty, are cold as ancient stone,
Their wooden walls whisper secrets they've known,
Of nectar and pollen, of sunlit days so fine,
Now locked away, like memories, in the mind's shrine.

My hands, rough from labor, trace the patterns laid,
By bees that have fled to some warmer glade.
Each scratch, each mark, tells a story of their flight,
A symphony of survival, played out in the light.

But what is left for me, in this season of frost?
A heart that yearns for the warmth it has lost.
For every bee that returns with spring's first kiss,
Is a promise of renewal, a chance at bliss.

Yet, here I am, guardian of an icy throne,
With only the wind for company, and the moon's lone moan.
I think of the queen, in her hidden retreat,
Dreaming of summers, where love and life meet.

Oh, how the heart aches, in this barren land,
To hold onto hope, with a trembling hand.
For even in winter, beneath the snow's deep sleep,
Life stirs, waiting, in a silent, secret keep.

And so, I wait, too, with faith unbroken,
Believing in the return of the spoken—
The hum of wings, the dance of the drone,
The sweet revival, when I am not alone.

Until then, I stand, a sentinel in the cold,
Guarding dreams, stories untold,
Of a world reborn, under skies of blue,
Where the honey flows, and the flowers renew.

title: blank verse meditation|time and memory
text:
I. The Hourglass  

Sand does not fall—it slips, a silent river,  
grain by grain unspooling what was held.  
The glass is cold, the neck too narrow for return.  
We watch, and call it measure—though it measures nothing  
but the watching. Light catches each descent,  
a flash, then gone: a name, a face, a door left open  
in some hallway of the mind no key can lock again.  

II. The Photograph  

Faded at the edges, curling like old skin,  
it holds them standing where the lilacs grew—  
her hat tilted, his hand half-raised, as if  
to shield his eyes from something not yet seen.  
Time did not pause; it pressed itself inside the emulsion,  
then walked away, leaving only this:  
the ghost of gesture, the weight of absence  
settling deeper with each year the paper thins.  

III. The Threshold  

I stand where yesterday meets tomorrow—  
not on solid ground, but on the breath between.  
Memory is not a room I enter, but the air  
I breathe inside it: dust-motes turning in slant light,  
familiar voices half-recalled, then lost  
like notes dissolving just beyond the ear.  
What remains is not the thing remembered,  
but the shape the longing makes in the hollow of now.

title: short nature essay in lyrical prose (about 300 words)|the first heartbreak
text:
The First Frost

It came not with thunder, but with silence—the kind that settles after the last leaf lets go. One morning, the world was still warm in memory; by afternoon, a thin, silver hush had spread across the grass, brittle and bright. I walked barefoot through it, toes stinging, breath pluming like a small, startled bird—unmoored.

The heartbreak was not a wound, but a weathering. Like bark splitting on an old maple in early November: slow, inevitable, revealing pale wood beneath the familiar grain. I watched myself from a distance—as if I were a riverbank, and the current, swollen with sudden rain, carried away stones I’d thought unmovable: my name spoken softly, a shared glance held too long, the weight of a hand resting just so on my shoulder. Gone. Not stolen. Simply… released, like dandelion clocks catching wind I hadn’t felt blowing.

Even the birds seemed quieter—not absent, but altered. Their songs thinned, became sparse as frost-etched twigs against a washed-out sky. I learned to listen differently: not for melody, but for the space between notes—the hollow where her laugh used to bloom like jasmine in June. That space grew tender with time, not empty, but *held*, like a seed pod waiting for thaw.

I gathered small things then: a feather shed by a mourning dove, a smooth stone worn by creek water, the curled, russet edge of a fallen oak leaf—each a quiet testament to endurance. Not healing, not forgetting, but becoming porous. Letting the cold in, yes—but also the light that slants low and golden across frozen ponds, turning them into mirrors of the bruised, beautiful sky.

This is how the earth teaches grief: not as ending, but as turning. The first frost does not kill the root. It asks the soil to remember its depth. It asks the stem to bend without breaking. And when spring returns—not with fanfare, but with a single, stubborn crocus pushing through black loam—I will not call it return. I will call it recognition: the quiet, green certainty that even the deepest ache can become fertile ground.

title: dramatic monologue|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
In the belly of the beast, where ovens roar
like lions at midnight, I stand and watch
the silverware clink like coins in a fountain,
each one a wish, a silent prayer to gods
who’ve never lifted a finger for us.

Here, beneath the chandeliers’ far-off glow,
our world is fire and grease, steam and sweat.
The bride’s laughter floats down from above,
a melody mixed with the hiss of onions
caramelizing on the grill. She knows not
the symphony of spatulas, the dance
of dishwashers, the rhythm of rolling pins.

Outside, they sip champagne under stars
that seem to wink at their borrowed bliss,
while we, the unsung, sculpt dreams from dough,
paint plates with sauces that speak of home,
of distant lands and forgotten flavors.
Each dish, a canvas; each fork, a brushstroke.

A waiter rushes by, tray balanced high,
carrying canapés like tiny ships,
sailing towards mouths that will never know
the hands that shaped them, the stories behind
each pinch of salt, each sprig of rosemary.

And when the night grows old, and the music fades,
we’ll scrape the remnants of their feast,
gather the crumbs of their happiness,
and sweep them away as if they were ours.
For here, in the kitchen, we are alchemists,
turning the mundane into magic, the simple
into something sacred, unseen but felt.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a mother's hands
text:
A Mother’s Hands  

O gentle hands, that cradle life anew,  
With veins like rivers carved by time and care,  
Whose calloused palms have borne both frost and dew,  
And smoothed each tear that fell in childhood’s air.  
They knead the bread, they mend the torn and frayed,  
They soothe the brow where fevered pulses race;  
In midnight hush, their quiet touch conveyed  
The sacred language no tongue can replace.  
No royal sceptre bears such sovereign grace,  
No sculptor’s chisel shapes with kinder art—  
These hands, though worn, hold heaven in their space,  
Each line a verse of love’s unbroken heart.  
So let the world praise strength in steel and stone—  
True power dwells where tender hands are known.

title: blank verse meditation|a soldier writing home
text:
Under the Canvas Sky

Beneath a canvas stretched wide and far,  
I lay, the earth my bed, stars my lamp.  
In this quiet, thoughts of home do stir,  
Of laughter, warmth, and familiar damp.  
My heart beats with the rhythm of the land,  
Yet yearns for the embrace of loving hands.

Words on Parchment

By the light of a flickering flame, I write,  
Each word a bridge from here to there.  
The ink flows, black as the night,  
Carrying hopes, dreams, and a soldier’s prayer.  
How can I capture the depth of my soul?  
When words feel shallow, a mere scroll.

Sealed with Hope

The letter folds, a promise held within,  
Sealed not just with wax, but with silent tears.  
May it find its way through battles’ din,  
To bring solace and quell all fears.  
Until then, under the vast, watchful sky,  
I wait, a guardian, dreaming of bygone lullabies.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|the first heartbreak
text:
The Day the Bluebird Flew Away

Once there was a child who loved a bluebird,  
Soft as sky, with wings like whispered words.  
Each morning, the bluebird perched on her thumb,  
Sang a song that made the whole world hum.  

She built a nest of twigs and thread,  
Filled it with sunshine, dandelion fluff, and bread.  
She whispered wishes, warm and low—  
“Stay with me. Please stay. Just so.”  

But one windy Wednesday, high and wide,  
The bluebird stretched its wings—and *glided*—  
Not to the oak, not to the hill,  
But over the fence, beyond the mill.  

The child stood still. Her chest felt tight,  
Like holding too much moonlight.  
No song came out. No tears would fall.  
Just quiet—soft, and very small.  

She watched the sky turn gold, then gray,  
And wondered: *Where do bluebirds go?*  
Then—*pitter-pat!*—a raindrop fell,  
Cool and kind, like saying, *It’s okay.*  

That night, she drew the bluebird’s shape  
On her window, with soap and tape.  
She named the space where it had been—  
A little room for love, unseen.  

Heartbreak is not an empty cup.  
It’s love that learned to hold itself up.  
And though the bluebird flew away,  
Her heart grew wider—day by day.

title: prose poem|an abandoned railway station
text:
The platform’s concrete tongue is cracked—not fissured, not fractured, but *unzipped*: a jagged black seam where asphalt bled up through the pour fifty years ago and never dried right.  

A single bench remains, bolted to the slab, its green paint blistered into miniature continents—peeling like sunburnt skin, revealing rust the color of dried blood under fingernails. A plastic grocery bag, fused to the armrest by heat and time, holds its shape: a translucent, crumpled lung.  

No pigeons. Just one sparrow, hopping sideways—not in panic, but with the deliberate, off-kilter gait of a man who’s just remembered he left the stove on. It pecks at a smear of something amber and viscous—not syrup, not tar—dripping from the underside of the overhang where a light fixture hung. The drip hasn’t moved in months. It’s *waiting*, not falling.  

The ticket booth window is gone. Not broken out—*removed*. Just an empty rectangle, framed in raw, honeycombed brick where mortar dissolved like sugar in rain. Inside, a single steel chair sits upright, legs planted, back tilted forward as if still listening to a voice that stopped speaking in 1978. Its vinyl seat is split open—not slashed, but *yawned*: a clean, dry tear revealing yellow foam that smells faintly of burnt almonds and wet newspaper left in a trunk.  

And the tracks? They don’t vanish into mist or weeds. They end. Abruptly. Cut off at the property line like a sentence severed mid-thought. Beyond them: a chain-link fence, sagging, strung with plastic ribbons—pink, blue, fluorescent green—tied tight around the posts. Not for ceremony. Not for warning. Just the kind of ribbon you’d use to mark a lost dog’s leash, or bind a bundle of rebar at a job site. Faded, frayed, snapping softly in a wind that carries the smell of hot transformer oil and crushed mint growing in the gravel.  

The station doesn’t hold memory.  
It holds *pause*.  
A breath caught between syllables.  
A door left ajar—not open, not closed—just *ajar*, hinge groaning low, continuously, like a throat clearing itself, over and over, for no one.

title: elegy|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Elegy for the Four Seasons of an Orchard

In spring, beneath the whispering boughs so light,
Where buds in tender green and blossoms white
Unfold like secrets kept from winter's night,
The orchard stirs with life, a gentle might.

Then summer comes, her arms full of sun,
Nurturing fruits till their sweet time is spun.
Under her gaze, each apple, peach, and plum,
Grows ripe and round, their promise now become.

But as the leaves begin to turn and fall,
Autumn whispers through the branches tall.
A bittersweet farewell, as one by one,
Fruits are gathered, and the season's done.

Winter then wraps the orchard in its shroud,
Bare limbs etched against the sky, unallowed
To bloom or bear, yet in this quiet cloud,
Rests the promise of what will be avowed.

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
First the kettle’s low growl—  
not a whistle, never a whistle, just that throaty,  
almost embarrassed hum as the water remembers it’s water again.  

Then the grind:  
burr grinder on the counter,  
left side slightly higher because the leg got chewed by the terrier in ’09,  
so the hopper tilts, and beans spill like tiny obsidian shrapnel onto the linoleum—  
I leave them. Let them wait. Let them be small black commas in the dim.  

The filter:  
not paper, never paper—  
a metal basket, dented where I dropped it into the sink last March,  
still holding the ghost of yesterday’s oil, faint as regret.  
I rinse it with cold water, not hot—  
hot makes the metal sigh, and I don’t want sighing yet.  

Coffee:  
Colombian, not from the fancy roaster downtown,  
but the one behind the laundromat on 7th,  
where Rosa weighs it out on a scale with peeling stickers—  
“28 grams,” she says, even if I don’t ask,  
even if my hair’s still damp from the shower,  
even if I’m wearing last night’s socks inside out.  

Water temp:  
just off boil—  
I count to seventeen after the click,  
then pour, slow, over the center,  
watch the bloom rise like a startled breath,  
brown and trembling, releasing something sharp and green,  
like crushed stems, like wet cedar bark,  
like the smell of the alley behind my father’s garage when I was twelve.  

First pour:  
circle, tight, deliberate—  
the grounds swell, darken, exhale steam that smells like burnt sugar and old letters.  

Second pour:  
wider, slower, spiraling down,  
water pooling at the edges,  
darkening the paper-thin rim of the filter,  
making the whole thing look like a small, breathing planet.  

Third pour:  
just enough to keep the bed submerged,  
no rush, no ritual—just water doing what water does,  
insistent, quiet, unimpressed.  

The drip:  
not steady. Never steady.  
A pause—three seconds—then a fat, glossy drop,  
then two quick ones, then silence again,  
like someone holding their tongue mid-sentence.  
I watch the carafe fill:  
amber at first, then deepening,  
staining the glass where the last batch dried into a ring—  
a permanent watermark, faint as a fingerprint.  

Steam rises:  
not straight, but curling left, always left,  
as if pulled by some private magnet—  
I’ve watched this for six years, three apartments,  
two breakups, one root canal,  
and it still curls left.  

The mug:  
chipped at the handle,  
glaze worn smooth where my thumb rests,  
blue glaze faded to the color of storm-light before rain,  
the kind that makes pigeons huddle on fire escapes.  

First sip:  
too hot, always too hot—  
I blow across the surface,  
not gently, but with the short, impatient puff of someone who’s already late for nothing,  
then taste:  
bitter yes, but also—  
the faintest echo of cherry pit,  
the memory of toasted oat,  
the mineral tang of the tap water filtered through the Brita pitcher whose lid hasn’t closed properly since Tuesday,  
so the charcoal’s gone soft, spongy, useless.  

Outside:  
streetlight still on, flickering low,  
casting long, liquid shadows from the fire escape bars onto the brick,  
a pigeon stirs on the ledge, fluffs one wing,  
doesn’t fly. Just watches. Or maybe it’s sleeping with one eye open.  
I don’t know. I don’t name it.  

The clock says 5:43.  
The neighbor’s cat is walking the fence again—  
paws silent, tail high,  
a slow, liquid S moving between the sagging wire and the rusted gutter.  

My left knee aches—not sharp, just there,  
like a quiet cousin who showed up uninvited and sat down.  

The coffee cools.  
Not all at once. In layers.  
The top loses heat first,  
then the middle,  
then the bottom, stubborn, thick, almost syrupy,  
holding warmth like a secret.  

I stir:  
spoon clinks—once, twice—  
not to mix, just to hear the sound,  
metal on ceramic,  
small, clear, unrepeatable.  

The light changes:  
not sunrise, not yet—  
just the sky thinning,  
gray softening to pearl,  
then to the pale, bruised blue  
that means the world is holding its breath,  
not waiting for anything,  
just… breathing.  

I drink.  
Not to wake up.  
Not to begin.  
Just because the cup is warm,  
and the steam has stopped rising,  
and the pigeon has flown,  
and the cat is gone,  
and the streetlight has died,  
and the coffee is still good,  
still bitter, still sweet in the aftertaste,  
still mine,  
still here,  
still dark,  
still steaming,  
still not quite enough,  
still exactly enough,  
still just coffee,  
just this,  
just now,  
just the quiet before the first door opens,  
before the first voice calls out,  
before the kettle forgets how to growl,  
before the day remembers its name.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
I. The Moon That Followed  
The moon rose round and silver-bright,  
Over tents of blue and white.  
It peeked through holes in canvas walls,  
And lit the path where little Nia crawled.  
She whispered, “Moon, you’re far away—  
But you came here to stay?”  
The moon just shone—soft, slow, and deep—  
And tucked her dreams beneath its keep.  

II. The Moon That Shared  
The moon split light like honey gold,  
A spoonful for the old, a spoonful for the bold.  
It warmed the tea in tin-cup hands,  
Gleamed on stones where children made their stands.  
When thunder rolled and winds blew low,  
The moon leaned close—and held them so.  
No passport stamped, no border crossed:  
Just quiet light, forever tossed.  

III. The Moon That Remembered  
The moon has seen a thousand lands—  
Deserts, rivers, sleeping sands.  
It knew the homes they left behind,  
The lullabies, the names, the kind  
Old grandmothers sang under trees,  
Now carried on the evening breeze.  
So when the camp grows still and thin,  
The moon hums back the songs within.

title: ode|a mother's hands
text:
Ode to a Mother's Hands

In gentle folds, where love and warmth reside,
A mother's hands, in grace, do softly guide.
They cradle dreams with tender, soothing touch,
And shape the world, for much is in their clutch.

From dawn till dusk, these hands, they never rest,
In every task, they find a way to bless.
With flour dusted, or soap suds high,
They teach us how to live, how not to lie.

In sickness, cool against a fevered brow,
Or warm, embracing, in a loving vow.
These hands, like roots, run deep and strong,
Binding hearts together, all life long.

Through years that pass, though skin may thin and pale,
The strength within, it never does fail.
For in each line, each crease, there lies
A story of a life, under kind skies.

title: dramatic monologue|learning a second language as an adult
text:
Tongue-Weight

Not the tongue—  
the *jaw*.  
That’s what buckles first:  
a hinge rusted shut in the attic of my skull,  
squeaking open only when I try to say *“rue”*—  
not the herb, but the street—  
and my molars grind down like subway brakes  
on a wet platform at 3 a.m.  

My throat doesn’t burn—it *hums*,  
a faulty transformer behind the drywall,  
vibrating the fillings in teeth that remember  
peanut butter sandwiches and spelling bees,  
not the guttural *ch* of *Bach*  
that sounds like a crow choking on its own shadow.  

I keep a notebook. Not for verbs, but for *failures*:  
—*“Je suis fatigué”* written in blue ink,  
then crossed out with a black line so thick  
it bleeds through to the next page,  
where I’ve drawn the exact shape of my left thumbnail  
after biting it raw during conjugation drills.  

My mouth collects foreign consonants like lint:  
they cling to the roof, fuzzy and staticky,  
until I sneeze—and out comes not *“pneumonie”*,  
but a burst of spit that lands on the subway map  
like a tiny, untranslatable stain.  

And the silence after I speak?  
It’s not empty.  
It’s full of the *other* words—  
the English ones, still warm, still breathing—  
pressing against the inside of my lips like hostages  
waiting for the wrong key to turn.  

Last Tuesday, I ordered coffee.  
Said *“un café, s’il vous plaît”*—  
clear, slow, precise.  
The barista smiled, nodded, turned—  
and poured my espresso into a paper cup  
already branded with a logo in Cyrillic.  
I didn’t correct her.  
Held the cup, warm as a bird’s egg,  
and watched the steam rise—  
not in spirals, not in clouds—  
but in three distinct, trembling columns,  
each one holding a different word I’d forgotten  
how to swallow.

title: blank verse meditation|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
The Moon Over a Refugee Camp  

No lantern hangs above the rows of tents—  
only the moon, cold and unblinking, pours  
its silver over dust that never settles,  
over tarps stretched thin as prayer, over faces  
half-erased by night and exhaustion.  
It does not choose its light: it falls on children  
curled like commas in the hollows of blankets,  
on mothers counting breaths instead of bread,  
on fathers mending wire with trembling hands,  
on the watchman who stares—not at the border,  
but up—where the same moon once rose  
above olive groves, above schoolyards,  
above roofs that held names and not numbers.  
No hymn is sung, no incense burns—  
yet something ancient answers in the stillness:  
the moon does not ask for papers or passports;  
it does not measure loss in square meters  
or divide the sky into zones of safety.  
It simply is—distant, constant, unowned—  
a silent witness, neither judge nor savior,  
casting its old, indifferent, tender light  
on all the earth’s unsheltered,  
on all the earth’s unmoored,  
on all the earth’s uncounted,  
as if to say:  
you are still beneath the same sky,  
you are still beneath the same moon,  
you are still beneath the same breath  
of the world—  
however broken,  
however bent,  
however far from home.

title: free verse poem|the night shift at a diner
text:
Under the neon hum, I stir,
Coffee brews, a dark and bitter truth,
The clock ticks, slow, like molasses in winter,
And here we are, the night owls, the dreamers, the lost.

Eggs sizzle on the griddle, a lonely symphony,
A man with eyes like storm clouds orders his usual,
Two over easy, toast, no butter, just jam,
He's been coming here for years, or so he says,
His stories blur, edges frayed, like the napkins.

Outside, the city sleeps, a heavy, silent beast,
But inside, it’s a carnival of whispers and clinks,
