A waitress with a heart-shaped locket smiles,
Her name tag reads "Sandy," but her smile is June,
She pours coffee, refills hope, one cup at a time.

The radio plays something old, something blue,
A song about love, or maybe just rain,
A young couple huddles in a corner booth,
Their fingers intertwined, a secret language,
They order pancakes, a stack of sweet beginnings.

I wipe the counter, a ritual, a prayer,
Traces of syrup, crumbs, and spilled dreams,
The diner is a sanctuary, a confessional,
Where every stranger has a story, a burden,
And the night shift, a quiet, endless vigil.

title: prose poem|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Autumn Leaves in a Cemetery  

They do not fall—they *drift*, as if remembering how to be light. A maple leaf, veined like a palm held open in surrender, lands on the cold stone of a name half-erased by lichen and time: *Eleanor, 1928–1994*. It trembles, not from wind, but from the hush that pools between headstones—thick as fog, thin as breath.  

Crimson, ochre, burnt umber: the trees above exhale their last gold. Each leaf is a small, brittle scripture—veins mapping forgotten rivers, edges curled like clenched fists softening in sleep. They gather in corners where the grass thins, where gravel gives way to earth’s quiet insistence. One sticks, damp and dark, to the bronze plaque of a soldier—*Beloved Son, Unbroken Promise*—its rust-red surface mirroring the tarnish on the metal, the slow, beautiful corrosion of all things held too tightly.  

A child’s red mitten lies abandoned near a chipped angel’s foot. No one retrieves it. The leaves ignore it. They settle instead on names, on dates, on the smooth curve of a weeping willow’s shadow stretched long and liquid across the path—like ink spilled over memory.  

You bend—not to pick one up, but to see the underside: pale, almost luminous, threaded with silver filaments. For a second, the leaf is not decay. It is translation: summer’s green heat rendered into something tender, transient, true. The air smells of wet bark and distant woodsmoke and the faint, sweet rot of apples left too long in an orchard.  

Somewhere, a crow calls—not a cry, but a pause. The leaves don’t answer. They simply lie, radiant in their letting go, writing no epitaph but this: *I was here. I was color. I was weightless.* And the earth, patient and unblinking, receives them—not as loss, but as return.

title: ode|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Ode to the Moon Over Al-Zatari

You rise—not over marble, nor cathedral spire,  
but over tents of tarp and fraying thread,  
over dust that drinks the day’s last fire,  
over children who count stars instead of bread.  

Your silver does not choose its light:  
it falls on folded blankets, rusted gates,  
on mothers stitching silence through the night,  
on maps drawn in the sand—then swept by winds’ late waits.  

You’ve watched Babylon fall, watched empires thin,  
yet hover now above this makeshift ground—  
no border on your face, no visa stamped within,  
no checkpoint where your cool, unblinking gaze is bound.  

You do not mourn the homes they left behind,  
nor praise the hands that built this barbed-wire air—  
you simply *are*: a slow, enduring sign  
that wonder still outlives despair.  

So when the generators cough and fade to hush,  
and guards walk shadows sharp as broken glass,  
you pour your quiet over every rush  
of breath, each prayer whispered into grass.  

O ancient lamp—unowned, unbarred, unblamed—  
you do not save, yet never look away.  
You are the same moon that once lit David’s psalm,  
and lights, tonight, a boy who cannot name his way.

title: blank verse meditation|a beekeeper in winter
text:
In the hush of winter, when the world is a brittle shell,
the beekeeper stands, hands in pockets, breath a cloud
in the cold. The hives, silent monoliths, hold their secrets
tight as clenched fists. He thinks of the bees, not sleeping,
but clustering, a living ball, a slow dance of warmth.

His boots crunch on snow, each step a small betrayal
of the stillness. The trees, stripped to their bones,
watch with hollow eyes. A crow perches, a black note
on a frozen staff, and caws—a sound like old hinges
or the first crack in ice. The beekeeper nods, a greeting
to the keeper of other mysteries.

He touches the hive, feels the faint thrum, a heartbeat
under layers of wood and snow. Inside, the queen
dreams of spring, her body a promise. He imagines
the honeycomb, golden and intricate, a city in stasis,
waiting for the sun's return. The air is sharp, a blade
at the back of his throat, but he swallows it down,
tastes the cold, the silence, the unyielding patience
of things that endure.

title: pantoum|the sound of a train at night
text:
The freight train groans past the old brick mill—  
a low C-sharp shuddering in my fillings,  
windows rattling loose in their frames,  
my daughter’s stuffed rabbit tipped sideways on the sill.  

A low C-sharp shuddering in my fillings—  
I count the cars by the clack-clack-hiss,  
my daughter’s stuffed rabbit tipped sideways on the sill,  
her breath still warm against my shoulder.  

I count the cars by the clack-clack-hiss:  
third car’s rusted door swinging open,  
her breath still warm against my shoulder,  
and the smell of wet wool from last week’s rain.  

Third car’s rusted door swinging open—  
I remember the conductor’s cap, bent at the brim,  
and the smell of wet wool from last week’s rain,  
the way my father hummed off-key in the garage.  

I remember the conductor’s cap, bent at the brim,  
the coffee gone cold in the chipped mug,  
the way my father hummed off-key in the garage,  
and how the tracks gleam, slick and black, just past the oak.  

The coffee gone cold in the chipped mug—  
my thumb rubs the chip near the handle,  
and how the tracks gleam, slick and black, just past the oak,  
the sound already thinning, already gone.  

My thumb rubs the chip near the handle,  
windows rattling loose in their frames,  
the sound already thinning, already gone,  
the freight train groans past the old brick mill.

title: villanelle|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
In spring, the orchard wakes with tender bloom,
Beneath the apple boughs, a soft romance.
The earth drinks deep of April's sweet perfume.

Summer crowns each branch with emerald plume,
Ripe fruits like secrets in the leafy dance.
In spring, the orchard wakes with tender bloom.

Autumn's gold whispers under the moon's loom,
Each fallen leaf a sigh, a slow expanse.
The earth drinks deep of April's sweet perfume.

Winter wraps its silence, stark and groom,
Yet dreams of blossoms in a quiet trance.
In spring, the orchard wakes with tender bloom.

Through cycles turning, life and love consume,
From seed to fruit, a timeless, graceful prance.
The earth drinks deep of April's sweet perfume,
In spring, the orchard wakes with tender bloom.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
I. Steam Rising  
The first pour—dark and trembling—  
curls like a question mark above the mug.  
You hold it in both hands,  
not drinking yet, just letting warmth seep  
into your knuckles, your wrists, your quiet pulse.  
This is not caffeine yet.  
This is the world holding its breath  
with you.

II. Light at the Edge  
Outside, the sky softens—  
a slow rinse of pearl and rose—  
while inside, steam thins to almost-nothing.  
You watch the light touch the rim of the cup,  
then your forearm, then the dust motes turning  
in the air like tiny, unhurried stars.  
No one else is awake.  
No one else needs you.  
For these minutes, you are allowed  
to be only this: warm, watching, unasked-for.

III. The First Sip  
It’s bitter. It’s rich. It’s real.  
You taste the earth, the fire, the waiting.  
And as the heat travels down your throat,  
something loosens—not all at once,  
but like a knot remembering how to yield.  
You are not fixing anything yet.  
You are simply here,  
awake before the day remembers you,  
and that is enough.

title: ode|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Sunday Afternoon, Main Branch  

The air smells of dust motes  
and the slow, sweet rot of paperbacks—  
not decay, exactly, but the damp  
breath of old glue softening in spines.  

A toddler drags a plastic dinosaur  
across the polished floor:  
*skkkt-skkt-skkt*—a tiny tank  
crossing a neutral zone.  

At Carrel 7B, a man sleeps  
with his forehead pressed to a Dewey Decimal  
catalog card still clutched in his fist—  
the ink smudged blue, like a bruise  
on his thumb.  

Sunlight slants through the high windows,  
cutting the room into amber slices—  
in one, a woman’s wrist vanishes  
beneath the glow of her laptop’s hinge;  
in another, a stack of returned biographies  
leans, slightly drunk, against a returns cart.  

The librarian at the front desk  
peels a strip of dried gum  
from under the circulation scanner—  
a translucent, amber fossil  
she folds once, twice, tucks  
into the hollow of her palm.  

No hush here. Just the low hum  
of the HVAC breathing deep,  
the *thunk* of a dropped book  
three aisles over—  
and the quiet, constant sound  
of pages turning,  
not like wings, not like prayers—  
but like something small  
and stubborn,  
unfolding.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Beekeeper's Winter Song

In a village where snowflakes dance and twirl,
Lived a beekeeper, kind and wise, in a swirl.
His bees were snug, their hives so tight,
Dreaming of flowers, in the cold winter night.

He wrapped them warm, with love and care,
Whispering secrets to the crisp, frosty air.
"Sleep now, my friends, till spring’s first bloom,
When sunshine returns and chases away the gloom."

Outside his door, the world was white,
But inside, by the fire, it was cozy and bright.
He read his books, with pages old,
Of bees and honey, and stories untold.

One day, a knock on his wooden door,
A tiny voice, barely more than a roar.
"Kind sir, can you spare a crumb or two?
I’m lost and hungry, I don’t know what to do."

The beekeeper smiled, his heart full of cheer,
Opened the door to a shivering deer.
"Come in, dear friend, and share my tea,
For kindness warms even the coldest sea."

Together they sat, the deer and the man,
Sharing tales of the forest, and plans for the land.
As the fire crackled, and the snow fell soft,
They dreamed of spring, when the earth would be aloft.

And when the deer left, with a thankful nod,
The beekeeper knew his heart was well trod.
For in giving warmth, he found his own,
A lesson learned, never to be alone.

So if you’re ever in a winter’s plight,
Remember the beekeeper, and let your kindness light.

title: short lyric poem|a soldier writing home
text:
Dear Ma,  

The ink’s smudged—blotted the “o” in “home”  
when the tent flap flapped open & rain came in sideways.  
Saw a robin today, fat as a dumpling,  
hopping near the latrine trench.  
Remember how you’d shoo them off the currant bush?  
I kept watch for ten minutes just to see it peck.  

My left boot’s sole’s coming loose—stitched it twice with thread  
from a torn sleeve of Higgins’ shirt (he don’t mind, says it’s “war tax”).  
The tea’s weak as dishwater, but I saved three lumps  
in my tobacco tin—still wrapped in that blue paper  
you used for the Christmas fudge.  

Tell Billy his slingshot’s in my pack, bent a little  
where he tried to shoot the church steeple last spring.  
I haven’t fired mine in three days. Not counting practice.  

This paper’s stiff—must’ve been stored in the supply tent  
with the damp sacks of flour. Smells like yeast & mildew.  
I’ll stop now. The light’s gone thin.  

—Eli

title: short nature essay in lyrical prose (about 300 words)|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The Kitchen’s First Breath  

Before light finds the sill, before the kettle sighs—  
it is *smell* that wakes me: warm yeast blooming like a slow white flower,  
cinnamon unspooling its rust-red thread through steam,  
brown sugar caramelizing at the edge of a cast-iron pan—  
a low, honeyed burn, almost sorrowful.  

I step barefoot on cool linoleum, cracked like old riverbeds,  
and there she stands—back bent, apron dusted with flour as fine as moth wings,  
her wrists knotted with time, yet moving with the quiet certainty of roots.  
The stove hums. A wooden spoon rests in a bowl of batter,  
its curve holding a dollop of gold, trembling.  

Outside, rain taps the windowpane—soft, insistent—  
but inside, the air is thick with memory made tangible:  
the nutty breath of toasted walnuts,  
the green sharpness of bruised mint from her windowsill pot,  
the deep, damp-earth musk of dried porcini steeping in cream.  
Even the clock smells—old wood and beeswax,  
its ticking muffled by the weight of scent.  

She never speaks of love. She folds it instead:  
into dumpling dough, into the careful twist of a cinnamon roll,  
into the way she lets the jam cool just long enough—  
not too hot, not too cold—before she spreads it, slow and sure,  
on bread still singing with oven-heat.  

And when I close my eyes, it is not her voice I hear first,  
but the *hush* before the crust cracks—  
that fragile, golden tension—  
and the sudden, sweet surrender of steam rising,  
carrying with it the whole grammar of belonging:  
flour, fire, patience, hands that remember  
what my tongue has forgotten how to name.  

This is where language begins—not in words, but in aroma:  
a vapor of vanilla and vigil,  
of burnt sugar and unspoken tenderness,  
rising, always rising—  
not toward heaven, but toward the throat,  
where hunger and holiness taste the same.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Spring's Awakening

In spring, the orchard dons its green attire,
Where buds and blooms in tender dance appear.
The sun, a gentle painter, sets on fire
Each petal soft, each leaf that whispers near.
The air, a fragrant nectar, sweetly flows,
As bees, like tiny maestros, hum their tunes.
The earth, with life, beneath the branches stirs,
And from the soil, new hopes and dreams are sown.

Yet in this scene of beauty, time does race,
For every bloom must face the fleeting day.
But while it lasts, the orchard finds its grace,
And in each bud, a promise starts to sway.

 Summer's Bounty

When summer spreads its golden, warming light,
The orchard swells with fruits of ripened hue.
The apples, pears, and plums, in full delight,
Hang heavy on the boughs where once they grew.
The days, now long, stretch out in lazy ease,
And children’s laughter fills the dappled shade.
The orchard’s heart beats strong, as if to please
The hands that tend and nurture, unafraid.

Yet even here, the shadows start to creep,
As evening falls and stars begin to show.
The night, a quiet watchman, comes to keep
The orchard safe, where secrets softly grow.

 Autumn's Harvest

Now autumn paints the leaves in amber gold,
A tapestry of reds and oranges bright.
The orchard yields its treasures, young and old,
As baskets fill with harvest’s pure delight.
The air, a crisp and cool embrace, invites
Reflection on the year that’s nearly done.
The branches, bare, stand proud against the nights,
Their work complete, their bounty fully won.

But as the leaves fall softly to the ground,
A sense of loss and change begins to rise.
Yet in this end, a new beginning’s found,
For winter’s rest will bring another rise.

title: spoken-word poem|watching a parent grow old
text:
Witness

I watch you shrink—  
not like a balloon losing air,  
but like a photograph left too long in sun:  
edges curling, colors softening,  
the sharp lines of your jaw blurring into mist.  

Your hands—once steady enough to stitch a torn kite,  
to steer a car through midnight rain,  
to hold my fevered forehead like a vow—  
now tremble when you lift the teacup.  
A small quake. A quiet betrayal.  
I don’t reach to steady it.  
I hold my breath instead.  

You forget where you left your glasses—  
but not how to hum the lullaby you sang me  
when thunder shook the walls.  
You misname the neighbor’s dog—  
yet still call me *my little sparrow*,  
same voice, same tenderness,  
as if time carved everything else away  
but the heartwood of love.  

I see the new silence between your sentences—  
not emptiness, but echo.  
Years pooling there, deep and slow.  
And I catch myself counting your steps  
like a child learning to count stars:  
one, two… then stopping, afraid  
to reach the end of the sky.  

You are not fading.  
You are folding—  
like origami worn thin by decades of careful hands,  
each crease a story, each fold a season,  
until what remains is something smaller,  
more fragile,  
and infinitely more sacred:  
the pure, unguarded shape of your soul,  
finally unburdened by having to hold us all up.  

So I sit beside you in the quiet light,  
not fixing, not rushing, not looking away—  
just witnessing.  
Not watching you grow old.  
But honoring how deeply,  
how fiercely,  
you have lived.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The Piano on the Pavement  

On a Tuesday, gray and slow,  
Sat an old piano—brown as dough—  
Left upon the pavement’s edge,  
With a cracked lid, yellowed pledge.  

Wind hummed low through its loose strings,  
Dust-danced soft on wooden wings.  
Sparrows pecked at ivory keys,  
Chirping, *“Who will play with me?”*  

Lily passed—it caught her eye—  
Not a box, not trash, but *why?*  
She tapped one key: a sleepy *plink!*  
A silver note rose—thin and pink!  

Then rain came down in silver drops,  
Tapping rhythms on its top.  
Frogs joined in from puddle-deep,  
*Plonk! Plonk! Plonk!*—a lullaby to keep.  

Night arrived with firefly light,  
Crickets strummed the strings so tight—  
*Zzzzt… zzzzt…* a whispery tune—  
Beneath the watchful, winking moon.  

Next dawn, Lily brought her friends—  
Three small hands, two drumsticks, ends  
Of bamboo flutes and tin-can drums—  
They made the old piano *thrum!*  

No one knew who left it there,  
But now it sang beyond compare:  
Not for show, nor fame, nor gold—  
Just for stories, warm and bold.  

So if you see a piano bare,  
Waiting quiet in the air—  
Stop and listen, soft and near…  
It’s not broken. It’s *just waiting here.*

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|the night shift at a diner
text:
In the diner, under the neon hum,
where the coffee never stops, and the night is just begun,
in the diner, where the streetlights cast their glow,
and the patrons, they come and go.

In the diner, where the waitress knows your name,
and the cook flips pancakes like he's putting out a flame,
in the diner, where the vinyl seats are cracked,
and the jukebox plays a song you half-remembered, almost fact.

In the diner, where the truckers stop to rest,
their eyes heavy, their stories best,
in the diner, where the old men sit and chat,
over eggs and toast, the hours pass, no need for that.

In the diner, where the students pull all-nighters,
books spread wide, dreams of futures brighter,
in the diner, where the loners find a home,
a place to be, a place to roam.

In the diner, where the couple whispers sweet,
their hands entwined, their love complete,
in the diner, where the regulars hold court,
over pie and coffee, their lives in full support.

In the diner, where the clock ticks slow,
and the night outside, it starts to grow,
in the diner, where the neon sign flickers,
a beacon in the dark, a light that lingers.

In the diner, where the waitress pours another cup,
her smile weary, her feet sore, but not yet up,
in the diner, where the cook wipes his brow,
the grill still hot, the night still now.

In the diner, where the stories intertwine,
lives overlapping, moments align,
in the diner, where the night shift reigns,
and the world outside, it fades, remains.

title: villanelle|drought on a family farm
text:
Drought on the Henderson Farm  

The creek bed gapes—a cracked and blanched white bone,  
The corn stands stiff in rows of brittle grey;  
No rain has kissed this soil for months, not one.  

The well rope frays where thirsty hands have thrown  
Their weight against the dry air, day by day.  
The creek bed gapes—a cracked and blanched white bone.  

Grandpa’s boots sink deep in dust, not loam—  
His knuckles whiten on the rusted plough.  
No rain has kissed this soil for months, not one.  

The barn door sags, its hinges sharp with groan;  
Inside, the calves lie still beneath the bough  
Of a creek bed gapes—a cracked and blanched white bone.  

Ma wipes her brow with cloth gone stiff and worn,  
Her eyes trace clouds that pass—but never stay.  
No rain has kissed this soil for months, not one.  

At dusk, the boy digs where the willow’s torn  
Roots coil like prayers half-lost in disarray.  
The creek bed gapes—a cracked and blanched white bone.  
No rain has kissed this soil for months, not one.

title: blank verse meditation|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
I. The Before  
The ovens hum low, a steady, patient thrum—  
not prayer, but heat made audible.  
We move in silence broken only by the scrape  
of knives on steel, the hiss of steam escaping  
from the stainless throat of the combi-oven.  
Flour dust hangs like suspended time.  
Outside, the garden laughs and clinks its glasses;  
in here, we count the minutes in butter-softened  
and the precise, unspoken weight of each tart shell.  
No names are spoken—only “the bride’s cake,”  
“the groom’s favorite,” “the gluten-free tray.”  
We know them by their absences:  
the empty chairs at the head table,  
the untouched champagne flutes stacked like promises  
waiting to be lifted, then emptied.

II. The During  
A rush—a door swings, a voice calls *“Plates up!”*—  
and suddenly the kitchen breathes faster.  
Steam rises in veils from the pass,  
where plating is a kind of quiet choreography:  
microgreens placed with tweezers, sauce drawn in arcs,  
each plate a small, perfect world we will not enter.  
We hear the muffled swell of strings,  
a pause, then laughter—warm, close, unfamiliar.  
Someone wipes sweat with a sleeve, checks the clock,  
and says, *“They’re cutting now.”*  
No one looks up. We plate the next course.  
The wedding is a rhythm we serve, not witness—  
a pulse measured in seconds between orders,  
in the clean line of a rim wiped, a garnish set just so.

III. The After  
Dishes pile like fallen monuments.  
The last guest has gone, the music folded into memory.  
We mop the floor where spilled wine dried to rust,  
stack chairs that held strangers turned tender,  
sweep crumbs from the path where vows were walked.  
In the walk-in, the leftover cake sits under foil—  
frosting slightly dimpled, tiers still proud.  
One pastry cook lifts a fork, tastes the vanilla bean,  
says nothing. The dishwasher roars its long, wet hymn.  
We pack our bags. No bouquet is thrown our way.  
But as we step into the cool street, dawn’s first light  
gilds the alley bricks—and for a breath,  
the silence feels less like absence,  
more like something shared,  
and softly, finally,  
ours.

title: elegy|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
The glove’s still there—  
not draped, not slumped, but *stuck*:  
thumb hooked like a fisherman’s barb  
on the splintered lip of the third post.  

Finger-tips hollowed into cupped ashtrays,  
palm a crumpled map of salt-stain constellations—  
last winter’s grit still gritting in the seams.  

Wind doesn’t take it. Rain just polishes the knuckle-bone  
where the leather’s worn thin as a moth’s wing  
over something that used to be warm.  

A squirrel paused yesterday, sniffed the cuff,  
then backed away, tail twitching—  
not fear, exactly. More like recognition  
of an object that has outlived its own utility,  
its own grammar.  

No hand will return for this.  
Not the one that lost it mid-swing,  
not the one that might’ve claimed it later,  
not even the cold, patient hand of rust  
creeping up the post’s iron spine.  

It hangs. Not mourning. Not waiting.  
Just *there*—  
a small, brown parenthesis  
in the sentence of the fence,  
the field, the slow, unblinking sky.

title: free verse poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The aluminum boat’s scuffed blue paint—  
peeling at the gunwale where his knee always rests.  
He doesn’t say *hold the pole steady* or *don’t drop the sinker in your shoe*—  
just hands me the Zebco 33, its plastic grip cracked like old river clay,  
and taps the reel with one knuckle. *Click.*  

We sit.  
His thermos leaks coffee onto the floorboard—brown stain shaped like West Virginia.  
I count the rust spots on the oarlocks.  
He chews Wrigley’s Spearmint, slow, never spits, just swallows the gum whole sometimes.  
I saw him do it once. Swallowed it like a stone.  

A dragonfly lands on his wrist. Doesn’t fly off.  
He doesn’t flick it. Just watches its wings catch light—  
thin as cellophane, trembling.  
My line goes slack. I yank it up: hook bent, worm gone,  
just a smear of pink pulp clinging to the barb.  

He nods at the water. Not at me.  
Not *try again*. Not *patience*.  
Just the nod—like he’s agreeing with something the current said.  

Later, rain starts—not hard, just that misty kind that makes the bass jump  
and the willows drip like tired monks.  
He unzips his flannel, pulls out a sandwich wrapped in wax paper:  
bologna, yellow mustard, two dill pickle chips tucked in the corner.  
Hands me half. No napkin. I eat it, salt and vinegar sharp on my tongue,  
and watch a heron stalk the reeds downstream—  
long legs, no hurry, no sound.  

When we pull in, the motor coughs twice, dies.  
He hauls the anchor, chain clanking,  
and I hold the bow against the dock piling—  
wet wood, green slime, the smell of drowned leaves and diesel.  
He steps off first. Boots thud on the planks.  
I follow. He walks ahead, shoulders hunched,  
one hand still in his pocket,  
the other holding the empty thermos by its dented lid.  

No goodbye.  
Just the screen door slamming behind him—  
that same warped hinge, same groan,  
every time.

title: sequence of haiku|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
Ring breaks the still night,
Voice from years past, soft and clear,
Heart leaps, time rewinds.

Whispers through the line,
Echoes of our childhood games,
Laughter in the dark.

Silence holds a weight,
Unspoken words, shared sorrow,
Tears blur distant stars.

title: poem in tercets|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
Ignition  
The key turns—engine hums, a low, warm thrum.  
Her small hands grip the wheel, knuckles white and tight.  
I rest my palm just above her trembling hand.  

Steering  
Left foot lifts—clutch bites, gear slides home with grace.  
She breathes in, lets the car roll forward slow.  
The road unspools like something she must trace.  

Letting Go  
My hand withdraws. The wheel steadies in her hold.  
She shifts, checks mirrors, signals, turns the curve—  
and for the first time, drives without me told.

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|a jazz club in the rain
text:
The Blue Hour at Muddy’s

Rain on the awning—  
rain on the brick face of the building—  
rain on the slick black street where taxis hiss past like startled cats—  
rain on the fogged-up window where a single smudge, a thumbprint, blurs the neon sign: MUDDY’S—  
rain on the fire escape where a stray cat licks its paw and watches the light leak out—  
rain on the awning—  
always the rain on the awning—

Inside:  
the low thrum of the bass—  
the bass that doesn’t walk but *swims*, thick as river silt—  
the bass that holds the room underwater and lets us breathe anyway—  
the bass that hums in your molars, your kneecaps, the hollow behind your ear—  
the bass that remembers every blues you ever swallowed whole—  

Inside:  
the saxophone—  
a cry bent sideways into smoke—  
a laugh caught mid-sob—  
a confession whispered into a whiskey glass—  
a question with no period, only commas, ellipses, breath—  
a phrase repeated three times, each time lower, slower, older—  
a melody that unbuttons its own collar and leans in close—  

Inside:  
the piano—  
ivories like river stones worn smooth by decades—  
chords that bloom like ink dropped in water—  
a left hand that walks the stairs backward, then forgets the landing—  
a right hand that sketches angels in the air before erasing them—  
a solo that starts in C minor and ends somewhere east of dawn, north of memory—  

Inside:  
the drummer—  
brushes whispering across snare like dry reeds in wind—  
sticks clicking time like clockwork crickets—  
a rimshot that cracks the silence like a snapped branch—  
a hi-hat sizzle that lifts the whole room two inches off the floor—  
a solo that isn’t about speed but about *weight*: the weight of waiting, the weight of wanting, the weight of a man who’s loved too hard and lost too often—  

Inside:  
the bartender—  
wiping the same spot on the bar for forty-three years—  
pouring bourbon neat, no ice, no questions—  
knowing whose grief needs sugar, whose rage needs rye, whose joy needs nothing but space—  
nodding when you don’t speak—  
remembering your mother’s name though you never told him—  
sliding a napkin across the bar with one word written in ballpoint: *breathe*—  

Inside:  
the patrons—  
the woman in the violet dress tracing the rim of her glass with one red nail—  
the old man in the corner booth whose hat never leaves his lap, whose eyes never leave the bandstand—  
the student with notebook open, writing not notes but fragments: *the way the light catches dust above the upright bass*, *how silence after the last note hangs like wet wool*—  
the couple holding hands under the table, fingers interlocked so tight their knuckles bleach white—  
the man who comes in every Tuesday at 9:17 p.m., sits alone, orders coffee, and closes his eyes until the second set ends—  
the girl who came in crying, stayed for three songs, left with her coat buttoned wrong and her shoulders lighter—  

Inside:  
the air—  
thick with cigarette smoke from twenty years ago, still lingering in the rafters—  
heavy with the scent of spilled beer and burnt sugar and leather chairs warmed by bodies—  
damp with breath and sweat and the slow exhale of surrender—  
alive with vibration—the ceiling fan shuddering, the floorboards sighing, the glass ashtrays trembling faintly in time—  

Outside:  
rain on the awning—  
rain on the fire escape—  
rain on the puddle where a streetlight bleeds gold—  
rain on the newspaper abandoned on the bench, words dissolving into ink rivers—  
rain on the bus shelter where two strangers share silence and the same narrow roof—  
rain on the awning—  
always the rain on the awning—

And the music—  
the music that doesn’t stop for umbrellas or traffic or heartbreak—  
the music that builds bridges between seconds—  
the music that turns longing into rhythm, loneliness into resonance, exhaustion into elevation—  
the music that says: *you are here, you are heard, you are part of the pulse, even when you think you’re just passing through*—  
the music that doesn’t ask you to be whole—  
only to be present—  
only to lean in—  
only to let the rain fall outside while the blue hour holds you inside—  
only to let the bass hold you—  
only to let the saxophone find the crack in your chest and pour light through it—  
only to let the piano remind you that every ending is also a breath before the next chord—  
only to let the drummer say, again and again, *yes, yes, yes—this moment counts—this breath matters—this ache is sacred—*  

Rain on the awning—  
rain on the awning—  
rain on the awning—  
and inside, always inside, the blue hour breathing,  
the band playing,  
the world turning,  
soft and stubborn,  
on a hinge of rain and resonance.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|hope after a long illness
text:
In a room where shadows played,
Lived a child, both brave and gray.
Through the window, light would pour,
Dancing on the worn-out floor.

Birds outside sang songs so free,
Tales of skies and leafy trees.
While inside, the child would dream,
Of rivers wide and meadows green.

One by one, the days went slow,
Like snails that leave their silvery flow.
But in whispers, soft and true,
Hope crept in with morning dew.

A tiny sprout, unseen, unbidden,
Pushed through cracks where light had hidden.
Day by day, it grew so tall,
Reaching out to touch the wall.

"See," said Mama, "how it stands?
Strong and steady, in these hands."
And the child, with eyes aglow,
Felt a warmth they'd long forgot.

Nightly stars, like glowing beads,
Wove a tapestry of deeds.
Dreams took flight on wings of night,
Carrying the child's delight.

Then one morn, the sun did beam,
Brighter than the wildest dream.
Feet found strength, and heart found cheer,
As laughter danced from ear to ear.

Out the door, with steps so light,
The child embraced the world's first sight.
Grass beneath, sky up above,
Life was brimming, full of love.

So remember, when the dark,
Whispers fears and leaves its mark,
Hope is there, a steadfast friend,
Growing strong till darkness bends.

title: elegy|grief after a dog dies
text:
Elegy for a Silent Friend  

The leash hangs slack upon the hook—  
a coil of absence, stiff and cold.  
Your bowl still holds the ghost of kibble,  
dust motes dancing where your nose once rolled.  

I walk the path we took at dawn,  
but now the rhythm stumbles, thin—  
no eager tug, no tail’s bright grammar,  
no warm weight leaning in, within.  

Your bed lies folded, soft and hollow,  
a crater where your dreaming lay.  
I find a single grizzled hair  
caught in the weave—and turn away.  

The world insists on light and motion:  
cars hum, birds call, the sky stays blue.  
How cruel the sun—to shine unchanged  
while all my compass points to you.  

No grand lament, no marble verse—  
just this: the hollow where your sigh  
would rise beside me in the dark,  
the silence after “Good boy. Goodbye.”

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|an abandoned railway station
text:
The Station That Held Its Breath  

The rails ran straight—then stopped.  
The signal arm hung low,  
a tired arm holding nothing but wind and sky.  

Brick walls wore coats of moss, soft as sleeping mice.  
Windows blinked with cracked glass,  
each pane a cloudy eye watching clouds drift by.  

A bench sat crooked, wood silvered by rain and years,  
its iron legs half-sunk in clover and dandelion fluff.  
A single blue tile—loose, bright, stubborn—  
still whispered *“Platform Two”* to the ants who marched across it.  

No whistle tore the air.  
No steam sighed from the throat of the old engine shed.  
Only the *shush-shush* of tall grass bowing,  
and the *tap-tap-tap* of a robin pecking at rust on the ticket booth’s brass knob.  

But sometimes—just before dusk, when light turns honey-thick—  
if you press your palm flat against the cold brick wall…  
you feel it:  
a slow, deep hum—not of wheels or wires,  
but of waiting.  
Warm as a buried heartbeat.  
Old as a lullaby half-remembered.  

The station didn’t forget the trains.  
It remembered the *hands*:  
small ones dropping candy wrappers,  
old ones gripping suitcases,  
tired ones waving goodbye until they were dots—then gone.  

So it held them all:  
the laughter that bounced off the vaulted roof,  
the tears that soaked into the floorboards,  
the quiet courage of departures,  
the sweeter ache of returns.  

Now the wild rose climbs the signal box like a girl climbing a friend’s back—  
and the station breathes in.  
And breathes out.  
And waits—  
not for steam or steel,  
but for the next soft footfall,  
the next wide-eyed pause,  
the next small hand reaching not for a ticket…  
but for wonder.  

*(The rails don’t end.  
They bend—into story.)*

title: poem in tercets|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Distant Glow

Smoke whispers to the twilight sky,
A silent signal, soft and high.
From afar, a story starts to unfold.

Embers' Dance

Flames leap in an eerie waltz,
Silhouettes against the night's pulse.
Each flicker, a secret told in gold.

Ashen Echo

Morning brings a hushed aftermath,
Charred remains where life once laughed.
The forest weeps in shades of gray.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Desert Stars, You  

You lie on cool sand,  
back hollowed by the earth’s slow breath,  
and the sky—oh, the sky—  
unfurls not as distance but as presence:  
a million cold fires breathing light that left its source  
before your first cry,  
before your first wound,  
before you learned to name loneliness.  

They do not judge your silence.  
They do not rush your healing.  
They simply *are*—ancient, steady, unblinking—  
holding space in the vast dark  
the way a mother holds a child who has forgotten how to rest.  

Let their light enter—not as answer, but as witness.  
Not as cure, but as kinship.  
You are not small beneath them.  
You are *of* them: stardust learning, at last,  
to feel the ground beneath it  
and the sky above it  
as one continuous grace.

title: ghazal|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The piano’s lid gapes like a gutted bass drum,  
its ivory keys yellowed—not with age, but nicotine stain.  

A squirrel nests in the pedal well, lined with foil gum wrappers,  
chews through felt hammers, leaves tiny tooth-marks on spruce grain.  

Rain pooled in the soundboard last Tuesday—still there,  
a shallow, trembling map of the neighborhood’s cracked sidewalks.  

One string hums D-sharp when wind lifts the storm door—  
not song, not sorrow: just rust vibrating inside its own coil.  

Its bench is gone, but two coffee rings bloom on the floorboards,  
ghosts of mugs held by hands that didn’t know they’d leave.  

I crouch. Press middle C. A thud, then silence—  
then, from the damp wool underbelly, the slow drip-drip-drip of pitch.

title: ballad in quatrains|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Title: The Morning Tide

In tunnels deep, where echoes play,
A train arrives at break of day.
The doors slide wide with metallic sighs,
As crowds pour in like human tides.

Beneath the earth, in steel cocoon,
We're swept along to morning's tune.
Pressed close, a sea of faces blend,
In silent pact, on time to bend.

Through stops and starts, we sway as one,
Bound by the tracks till journeys done.
Each mind adrift in thought or dream,
Till stations call, and paths they deem.

At last, the light, the world above,
We spill out, freed from crowded love.
Yet come tomorrow, once again,
This dance resumes, this moving train.

title: sequence of haiku|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Smoke like a bruise on the ridge—  
my coffee’s gone cold.  
That’s where I buried the dog last spring.  

Flare flares behind Hemlock Hill—  
not lightning, not sunset.  
The neighbor’s rooster won’t stop crowing.  

Ash on my tongue again.  
Tried to call Mom.  
Her line’s still dead from Tuesday’s storm.

title: elegy|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. The Threshold  
The door sighs open—cinnamon and yeast,  
a warm breath rising from the oven’s throat.  
Flour dust hangs like suspended time,  
and sugar glistens on her knuckles,  
soft as ash.  
I stand just there, barefoot on cool linoleum,  
not yet called in—  
already held.

II. The Simmer  
Onions weep in golden pools of butter,  
cloves bloom dark and sharp beneath steam,  
cumin whispers its ancient name.  
Her apron smells of yesterday’s bread,  
tomorrow’s jam,  
and the faint, metallic tang of the old kettle—  
always singing, never boiling over.  
I watch her stir, slow as a vow,  
the scent thickening the air  
until memory has no choice but to kneel.

III. The Hollow  
The stove is cold now.  
No crust cracks under gentle thumb,  
no vanilla ghosts the cooling rack.  
I open the pantry—dusty jars, dried lavender,  
a single cinnamon stick brittle as bone.  
The silence hums with absence,  
and when I close my eyes,  
the smell returns—not as it was,  
but as echo: warm, unrepeatable,  
gone before I can name it.

title: sequence of haiku|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Rainy Night Jazz

Whispers through the rain,  
Saxophone's soft cry lingers—  
Neon lights flicker.

Drops on cymbals dance,  
Piano keys sing in shadows—  
Night's cool, gentle touch.

Laughter mingles well,  
With the bass's deep heartbeat—  
Rain taps time along.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|teenage summer jobs
text:
You wiped grease off the fryer basket with a rag that smelled like burnt sugar and diesel—  
not honey, not maple, but *burnt sugar*, the kind that caramelizes on the underside of a waffle iron at 3 a.m.,  
when the walk-in hummed like a trapped wasp and the floor tiles held the ghost-heat of seventeen pairs of sneakers.  

You counted quarters into rolls, fingers sticky with syrup from the fountain gun’s leaky O-ring,  
and once, you watched a cockroach walk upside-down across the fluorescent fixture—  
its legs moving like tiny, precise tuning forks vibrating just below hearing.  

You learned the weight of silence between orders:  
not empty, but *charged*—like the pause before rain hits hot asphalt,  
or the half-second after a customer says *“Just water”* and you nod,  
and their knuckles whiten around the paper cup they didn’t ask for.  

No epiphany came with the last paycheck.  
Just the slow unclenching of your jaw.  
The way your shoulders finally remembered the shape of air.  
And how, years later, the scent of warm vinyl seats in a ’98 Camry  
still opens a door—not to nostalgia, but to the quiet certainty  
that you were already whole,  
standing there in the fluorescent glare,  
counting change,  
breathing,  
unfolding.

title: elegy|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The old clock ticks, a steady pulse in the night,
Echoes through stone and timber, winding tight.
Up here, in my tower, the sea wind's keen bite,
Wraps around me, a shroud, as I face the light.

Fingers worn, by time and touch, to bone,
Flip the switch; the lamp flares, like a heart alone.
Decades of silence, save for gulls' cries, drones,
Of waves that crash and whisper their sad tones.

This room, with its maps, faded, tattered, frayed,
Traces of storms long past, and ships once waylaid.
Each chart, each log, bears marks of days I've stayed,
A life poured out, in ink, now almost drained.

Outside, the stars hang low, like lanterns cold,
Guiding no one, in skies vast, dark, and old.
I think of her, who left, when the tide turned bold,
Taking with it, all the warmth, leaving just gold.

The beacon spins, casting light on waves that weep,
For sailors lost, and dreams too deep asleep.
My eyes, they water, but not from any creep
Of chill; instead, from memories I keep.

Tonight, the final watch, the last embrace,
Of shadows dancing on these walls, this place.
Tomorrow, strangers come, with faces new,
To man the light, and keep the night at bay, and true.

But I'll be gone, into the dawn's soft hue,
Carrying with me only what I knew:
The lighthouse's heart, its silent, steady beat,
And the ocean's song, forever at my feet.

title: dramatic monologue|a mother's hands
text:
Mother’s Hands  

Not the hands that cradle—soft as down,  
nor those that knead the bread at dawn—  
but these: knotted, veined, a map of salt and storm,  
trembling slightly as they lift the teacup,  
steam rising like a ghost between cracked knuckles.  

These are the hands that held me *through*—  
not just *up*, but *through*:  
through fever’s red tide, through the shudder of first loss,  
through the silence after the slammed door,  
through the hollow hours when I was gone  
and she stood at the sink, scrubbing the same plate  
three times, water cold, light thinning at the window.  

I remember the scar—a silver seam across the thumb—  
from the bread knife slipping on a Tuesday,  
while she hummed off-key, blood welling slow,  
and wiped it with her apron, never pausing the song.  
That scar is older than my graduation gown.  
Older than the letter I never sent.  

Look closer:  
the blue tracery beneath the skin isn’t just age—  
it’s the echo of every wrist she steadied,  
every forehead cooled with damp cloth,  
every small, sleeping head she smoothed  
without waking, without breath, without sound—  
as if love were a language spoken only in pressure,  
in heat, in the quiet weight of palm against temple.  

And now—  
now they rest, folded in her lap like tired birds,  
still shaped for holding,  
still remembering the curve of my skull,  
the exact angle of my elbow,  
the way my fingers used to thread through hers  
like roots finding soil.  

They do not ask for praise.  
They do not name their ache.  
They simply *are*:  
earth-worn, salt-stung,  
still warm  
where the world has worn them thin.

title: short nature essay in lyrical prose (about 300 words)|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
Shift’s Last Light

The clock exhales twelve hours—soft, slow, a sigh through cracked fluorescent veins. She unzips her scrubs like shedding skin: the starched blue peeling away from shoulders still humming with the tremor of IV pumps, the echo of a child’s fevered whisper, the weight of a hand held too long in letting go. Her shoes—scuffed white oxfords—hold the imprint of corridors walked in quiet urgency, floors polished to a hush that swallowed footsteps, alarms, sobs.

Outside, dusk is stitching gold through the maple’s thinning crown. She stands beneath it, breath deep as river water after rain—cool, clear, gathering itself. A sparrow flits low, wings a flicker of burnt umber; its small heart beats faster than hers now, steady at last. She watches a single leaf spiral down—not falling, but *unfurling*—a slow surrender to air, to gravity, to grace.

Her hands remember: the cool curve of a forehead, the fragile pulse at a wrist, the way light caught in an old man’s glasses as he smiled through morphine’s soft fog. They remember too the tremor before a code, the salt-taste of tears wiped hastily on a sleeve, the silent pact made with exhaustion—that she would stay, even when her bones whispered otherwise.

A breeze lifts the hair from her nape, cool as creek water over stone. She closes her eyes—not in weariness, but in listening: to the rustle of dry grass, the distant chime of wind bells from a neighbor’s porch, the slow, sure rhythm of her own returning breath. The world hasn’t stopped. It never does. But for this suspended minute, it holds its breath with her.

She walks home—not toward rest, exactly, but toward the quiet alchemy of return: steam rising from a kettle, the weight of a book in her lap, the slow unfurling of self, petal by petal, back into her own name. Night arrives not as absence, but as presence—deep, tender, and vast as the first stars pricking the violet sky. She carries no trophy, only this: the quiet certainty that tenderness, worn like armor and offered like water, leaves its own kind of light behind—soft, enduring, and wholly human.

title: ode|moving out of a childhood home
text:
In the room where light slants like a half-finished sentence,
I gather what’s left: a shoebox of letters, their edges
curling like old photographs, and the map you drew
with crayon continents, each one a promise of escape.

The house hums with the ghost of your laughter,
echoes trapped in the walls, a chorus of yesterdays.
I find your fingerprints on the window, smudged moons
in a sky that no longer remembers the stars we named.

Outside, the oak stands guard, its bark a braille
of secrets whispered to the wind. I press my palm
against it, feel the pulse of seasons passed—
each ring a year we grew apart, together.

In the garage, your bike leans against the wall,
tires flat, chain rusted, a monument to motion stilled.
I touch the handlebars, cold metal under fingertips,
and for a moment, we’re racing down the street again.

The key in my hand is heavy, a small piece of metal
that once unlocked everything. Now, it just fits
a lock that will soon belong to strangers. I turn,
the click a period at the end of a long, shared verse.

title: short untitled lowercase poem in the style of modern Instagram poetry books|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
insomnia & the fridge hum  

3:47 a.m.  
the house holds its breath—  
except the fridge,  
that low throaty thrum  
vibrating through the floorboard,  
up my bare feet,  
into my ribs.  

i stand in the blue spill of its light,  
door open like a confession,  
but there’s nothing i want—  
just the cold,  
just the sound,  
just the proof  
that something, somewhere,  
is still running.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|the ocean during a storm
text:
The sea isn’t blue tonight—it’s the colour of a bruise under thin skin, or that tarnished silver spoon my grandmother dropped down the sink in ’73 and never fished out. Rain comes sideways, stinging the salt-crusted windowpane where I press my forehead, cold glass fogging with breath I don’t quite remember taking. Outside, the breakers don’t crash—they *shudder*, thick and guttural, like something heavy dragged over gravel and wet rope.  

I smell ozone, yes, but also the damp wool of the sweater I wore yesterday, still draped over the chair, and the faint, sour tang of the single oyster I ate at noon—its shell still on the sill, half-full of rainwater, trembling. The gulls aren’t crying; they’re *hissing*, low and ragged, wings pinned tight against the wind’s fist. One landed on the roof earlier, just for a second—feathers ruffled, one leg lifted, staring not at the churning grey, but *in*, right through the slate, as if it knew about the loose floorboard near the bed, the one that creaks when I step on it barefoot at 3:17 a.m.  

Lightning doesn’t flash—it *unfurls*, slow and arterial, lighting the underside of the clouds like the inside of a fish’s mouth. For three seconds, I see the drowned pine leaning into the surf, its roots bare and white as knuckles. Then black again. My left thumbnail is split. I pick at it. Salt stings.  

The tide’s pulling back now—not retreating, exactly, but *withdrawing*, sullen, dragging pebbles like teeth across stone. Somewhere, a buoy clangs. Not rhythmically. Just once. Then silence, thick and wet, full of the sound of my own pulse behind my ears—and the distant, irregular thump of the neighbour’s washing machine, still running, though she’s been gone three weeks.

title: ghazal|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
In the hush of a library on a Sunday, whispers line each shelf,  
Silent tales unfold where light and shadow gently weave themselves.

A scholar's sigh mingles softly with the turning of a page,  
Lost in worlds of ink and time, where ancient heroes wage.

Sunbeams dance through dust, a quiet, golden ballet,  
On this tranquil stage, no soul dares to sway.

Here, in rows of bound adventures, dreams are laid to rest,  
Each book a door to secret realms, where every heart is blessed.

But outside, the world's loud rush seems far, a distant shore,  
In here, the hours slow, as peace and calm restore.

These walls, a fortress 'gainst the chaos of the day,  
Guardian of stories, in silence they will stay.

So come, find solace in the quiet, let your thoughts take flight,  
For in this sanctuary, even lost souls find light.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
I. The Hour Unspooled  
When midnight’s hush should cradle thought to rest,  
And weary bones sink deep in downy keep,  
I lie awake—the mind a restless guest—  
While silent hours stretch, cold and steep.  
The clock’s faint tick, a metronome unkind,  
Counts seconds lost to sleep’s unyielding door;  
My pulse beats loud, my body ill-defined  
Between the ache of wanting more—of more  
Than wakefulness. The world outside is stilled,  
Yet in my skull, bright fragments twist and swarm—  
A fevered script no reason has fulfilled,  
A shapeless storm without a name or form.  
So darkness holds me, wide-eyed, thin, and bare—  
No dawn yet earned, no peace, no tender air.  

II. The Hum Beneath  
Then—low, persistent—through the kitchen wall,  
A tremor stirs: the fridge’s steady drone,  
A bassline thrumming through the hollow hall,  
The house’s slow and ceaseless undertone.  
It does not plead, nor pause, nor seek reply,  
But hums its vow to chill the milk, the greens,  
To guard the perishable, calm and sly,  
While I count breaths that falter, thin, unseen.  
That hum—a thread of sound both deep and plain—  
Becomes the rhythm of my watchful state:  
Not lullaby, but witness to my pain,  
A faithful ghost behind the bedroom gate.  
It knows no tiredness; it needs no rest—  
It hums—and I am hummed into unrest.  

III. The Light Within  
At last I rise, drawn by that humming call,  
And open wide the fridge’s silver maw:  
A sudden flood—cold light on empty wall,  
On jars half-full, on wilted herbs’ soft flaw.  
No hunger guides me, only need to see  
Some proof the world still turns, still holds its place—  
This pale electric clarity, this key  
To time’s suspended, solitary space.  
The hum grows louder, warm against my ear,  
As if the machine itself now leans to speak:  
*You are not broken. You are simply here.*  
The light fades slowly as the door grows weak—  
I close it softly, carry back the glow—  
Not sleep, but grace: the quiet I now know.

title: pantoum|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The turnstile’s cold chrome bites my knuckle—  
a nickel’s worth of pressure, sharp and thin.  
A man exhales steam that smells of burnt toast and axle grease,  
his earbuds leaking bass like a drowned drum.  

A nickel’s worth of pressure, sharp and thin,  
presses the bus pass flat against my thigh.  
His earbuds leaking bass like a drowned drum,  
I watch a woman fold origami from a crumpled MetroCard.  

Presses the bus pass flat against my thigh—  
its magnetic stripe flaking, silver-gray and frail.  
She folds origami from a crumpled MetroCard:  
a crane with one wing bent, trembling, almost real.  

Its magnetic stripe flaking, silver-gray and frail,  
a toddler grips a strap, fingers slick with apple butter.  
A crane with one wing bent, trembling, almost real—  
the train lurches; her breath catches, then steadies.  

A toddler grips a strap, fingers slick with apple butter,  
while overhead, a speaker crackles: *“Next stop is not this one.”*  
Her breath catches, then steadies—  
and the doors sigh open on a wall of wet wool and silence.
